\begin{infobox}{Conventions (identical to the Question Paper)}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item $n$ qubits; a Pauli string is a word over $\{I, X, Y, Z\}$ whose character $k$ acts on qubit $k$; basis states $\ket{q_0q_1\dots q_{n-1}}$ are written
      \textbf{qubit 0 first}. $H = \sum_kc_kP_k$ with real $c_k$; $E_0$ = smallest eigenvalue; $E(\boldsymbol\theta) = \braket{\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)|H|\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)}$.
\item $R_Y(\theta) = e^{-i\theta Y/2}$, $R_X(\theta) = e^{-i\theta X/2}$, $R_Z(\theta) = e^{-i\theta Z/2}$, $S = \operatorname{diag}(1, i)$; CUDA-Q's \texttt{exp\_pauli(theta, q, word)} applies $e^{+i\theta P}$.
      Two-qubit matrices use the order $\ket{00}, \ket{01}, \ket{10}, \ket{11}$.
\item \textbf{Jordan--Wigner} (qubit $\ket1$ = occupied): $a_j^\dagger = Z_0\cdots Z_{j-1}\,\tfrac12(X_j - iY_j)$, $n_j = \tfrac12(I - Z_j)$.
\item \textbf{The notebook} (\texttt{VQE.ipynb}): default Ising chain $H = -J\sum_{i}Z_iZ_{i+1} - h\sum_iX_i$ (open, $N = 15$, $J = 1$, $h = 0.5$, 29 terms);
      hardware-efficient ansatz with $L = 2$ layers of [$R_Y$ on all qubits, CNOT ladder] plus a final $R_Y$ layer; COBYLA, 300 evaluations; exact
      energies via \texttt{cudaq.observe}. H$_2$ example: 4 qubits, 15 Pauli terms (STO-3G, Jordan--Wigner, spin-orbitals ordered $\sigma_g\alpha, \sigma_g\beta, \sigma_u\alpha, \sigma_u\beta$;
      coefficients correspond to $R = 0.740$ \AA), Hartree--Fock $\ket{1100}$, UCC state $e^{i\theta\,X_0X_1X_2Y_3}\ket{1100}$, FCI energy $-1.137284$ Ha.
      A \emph{previously recorded run} means the outputs stored in the notebook (CUDA-Q 0.16.0, CPU target \texttt{qpp-cpu}).
\item Energies of molecules in Hartree (Ha); 1 Ha $= 627.51$ kcal/mol; chemical accuracy $1.6$ mHa. Numerical answers are rounded.
\end{itemize}
\end{infobox}

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{1}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{$2\times2$ eigenproblem}
The ground-state energy (smallest eigenvalue) of $H = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\ 2 & -2\end{pmatrix}$ and a normalised eigenvector for it are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$-2$ and $(0, 1)^{\mathsf T}$ & \optlabel{B}\,$2$ and $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(2, 1)^{\mathsf T}$ \\[3pt]
\correctlabel{C}\,$-3$ and $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(1, -2)^{\mathsf T}$ & \optlabel{D}\,$-3$ and $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(2, 1)^{\mathsf T}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $-3$ and $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(1, -2)^{\mathsf T}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Eigenvalues from the characteristic polynomial; eigenvectors from the null space of $H - \lambda I$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\det(H - \lambda I) = 0$; $(H - \lambda I)v = 0$; normalise $v/\|v\|$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Characteristic polynomial: $\det(H - \lambda I) = (1 - \lambda)(-2 - \lambda) - 4 = \lambda^2 + \lambda - 6 = (\lambda + 3)(\lambda - 2)$,
so $\lambda \in \{-3, 2\}$ and $E_0 = -3$.
Eigenvector for $-3$: $(H + 3I)v = 0$ gives $4v_1 + 2v_2 = 0$, i.e.\ $v_2 = -2v_1$: $v = (1, -2)/\sqrt5$.
Check: $Hv = (1 - 4, 2 + 4)/\sqrt5 = (-3, 6)/\sqrt5 = -3v$. The vector $(2, 1)/\sqrt5$ is orthogonal to it and belongs to $\lambda = 2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $-2$ is the smallest \emph{diagonal} entry; off-diagonal coupling pushes the true minimum lower, to $-3$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $2$ is the largest eigenvalue, not the ground state.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $(2, 1)/\sqrt5$ is the eigenvector of the \emph{other} eigenvalue $2$: $H(2,1) = (4, 2) = 2(2, 1)$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The ground state lies below the smallest diagonal element whenever off-diagonal couplings exist.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{2}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Rayleigh quotient}
For the same matrix $H = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\ 2 & -2\end{pmatrix}$, the Rayleigh quotient $R(v) = \dfrac{v^{\mathsf T}Hv}{v^{\mathsf T}v}$ of the trial
vector $v = (1, -1)^{\mathsf T}$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$-5$, which lies below $E_0$ & \optlabel{B}\,$-3$, exactly $E_0$ \\[3pt]
\correctlabel{C}\,$-2.5$, which lies above $E_0 = -3$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.5$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $-2.5$, which lies above $E_0 = -3$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Rayleigh quotient and its bounds.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $R(v) = \frac{v^{\mathsf T}Hv}{v^{\mathsf T}v}$, $\ \lambda_{\min} \le R(v) \le \lambda_{\max}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $Hv = (1 - 2,\ 2 + 2) = (-1, 4)$, so $v^{\mathsf T}Hv = 1\cdot(-1) + (-1)\cdot4 = -5$, and $v^{\mathsf T}v = 2$: $R(v) = -5/2 = -2.5$.
The Rayleigh quotient of any non-zero vector lies between the smallest and largest eigenvalue: $-3 \le -2.5 \le 2$.
Eigenbasis check: with $u_0 = (1, -2)/\sqrt5$ (eigenvalue $-3$), the weight of $u_0$ in $v/\|v\|$ is $\langle v, u_0\rangle^2/\|v\|^2 = (3/\sqrt5)^2/2 = 0.9$;
the remaining $0.1$ belongs to eigenvalue $2$: $R = 0.9(-3) + 0.1(2) = -2.5$. This is the variational principle in its simplest form.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $-5$ is $v^{\mathsf T}Hv$ without dividing by $v^{\mathsf T}v = 2$; no Rayleigh quotient can lie below $\lambda_{\min} = -3$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $-3$ would require $v \propto (1, -2)$; $(1, -1)$ is not an eigenvector.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.5$ comes from sign errors in $Hv$; the correct $Hv = (-1, 4)$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Any trial vector's energy is an upper bound to the ground energy --- VQE in one line.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{3}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Trace, determinant, spectrum}
For the real symmetric matrix $M = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & 0\\ 1 & 2 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{pmatrix}$, match each quantity (List-I) with its value (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & $\operatorname{tr} M$ & \textbf{(1)} & $15$ \\
\textbf{(Q)} & $\det M$ & \textbf{(2)} & $1$ \\
\textbf{(R)} & smallest eigenvalue of $M$ & \textbf{(3)} & $9$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & largest eigenvalue of $M$ & \textbf{(4)} & $5$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$2 & \correctlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$2, S$\to$4 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$1, Q$\to$3, R$\to$2, S$\to$4 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$2, S$\to$4

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Trace = sum, determinant = product of eigenvalues; block-diagonal matrices.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\operatorname{tr}M = \sum\lambda_i$, $\det M = \prod\lambda_i$; $\begin{psmallmatrix}a&b\\b&a\end{psmallmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $a \pm b$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $M$ is block diagonal: the block $\begin{psmallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{psmallmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $2 \pm 1 = 1, 3$ (eigenvectors $(1, \mp1)/\sqrt2$), and the
block $(5)$ has eigenvalue $5$. Spectrum $\{1, 3, 5\}$.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item P: trace = sum of diagonal entries $= 2 + 2 + 5 = 9$ = sum of eigenvalues (3).
\item Q: determinant = product of eigenvalues $= 1\cdot3\cdot5 = 15$ (also $(4 - 1)\cdot5$) (1).
\item R: smallest eigenvalue $1$ (2) --- the ``ground state'' of $M$.
\item S: largest eigenvalue $5$ (4).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] R$\to$4, S$\to$2 swaps smallest and largest eigenvalues.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] P$\to$1, Q$\to$3 swaps trace and determinant: $9 = 2+2+5$, $15 = 1\cdot3\cdot5$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Q$\to$4, S$\to$1 gives the determinant 5 and the largest eigenvalue 15; the eigenvalues are only $1, 3, 5$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Check eigenvalues against trace and determinant.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{4}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Stationary states}
An energy eigenstate $\ket{\psi_E}$ of a time-independent Hamiltonian ($H\ket{\psi_E} = E\ket{\psi_E}$) evolves under the time-dependent
Schr\"odinger equation $i\hbar\,\partial_t\ket{\psi(t)} = H\ket{\psi(t)}$. Which statement is correct?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] $\ket{\psi(t)} = e^{-Et/\hbar}\ket{\psi_E}$: the state decays in time
\item[\optlabel{B}] The state is constant only if $E = 0$; otherwise it moves to other eigenstates
\item[\correctlabel{C}] $\ket{\psi(t)} = e^{-iEt/\hbar}\ket{\psi_E}$: only a global phase changes, so all measurement probabilities are constant in time
\item[\optlabel{D}] The probabilities oscillate with angular frequency $E/\hbar$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $\ket{\psi(t)} = e^{-iEt/\hbar}\ket{\psi_E}$: only a global phase changes, so all measurement probabilities are constant in time

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Stationary states; global versus relative phase.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\ket{\psi(t)} = e^{-iHt/\hbar}\ket{\psi(0)}$; on an eigenvector $e^{-iHt/\hbar}\ket{\psi_E} = e^{-iEt/\hbar}\ket{\psi_E}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The formal solution is $\ket{\psi(t)} = e^{-iHt/\hbar}\ket{\psi(0)}$. On an eigenvector $H$ acts as the number $E$, so
$e^{-iHt/\hbar}\ket{\psi_E} = e^{-iEt/\hbar}\ket{\psi_E}$ (expand the exponential as a power series). The factor has modulus 1: a
\emph{global} phase, invisible in every measurement. Hence eigenstates are called \emph{stationary states}, and finding them
reduces to the time-independent equation $H\ket\psi = E\ket\psi$ --- the eigenvalue problem VQE solves. A superposition of
eigenstates with different energies, by contrast, acquires \emph{relative} phases and its probabilities can oscillate.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $e^{-Et/\hbar}$ lacks the $i$: Schr\"odinger evolution is unitary, norms are conserved.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Eigenstates stay eigenstates for any $E$; only superpositions of different energies evolve non-trivially.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] A global phase has no observable effect; probabilities of an eigenstate do not oscillate.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Energy eigenstates are stationary: finding them is the time-independent problem $H\ket\psi = E\ket\psi$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{5}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Energy units, chemical accuracy}
Using $1\ \text{Hartree} = 627.51$ kcal/mol, an energy error of $0.005$ Hartree corresponds to about ... and is ... chemically
accurate (chemical accuracy: 1 kcal/mol $\approx$ 1.6 mHa).
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$3.14$ kcal/mol; not & \optlabel{B}\,$3.14$ kcal/mol; still \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$0.31$ kcal/mol; still & \optlabel{D}\,$125.5$ kcal/mol; not
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $3.14$ kcal/mol; not

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Energy units; chemical accuracy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $1$ Ha $= 627.51$ kcal/mol $= 27.211$ eV; chemical accuracy $1$ kcal/mol $= 1.594$ mHa.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $0.005 \times 627.51 = 3.138$ kcal/mol. Chemical accuracy means an error below $1$ kcal/mol $= 1/627.51$ Ha $= 1.594$ mHa
($\approx 1.6$ mHa, the threshold printed by the notebook). $5$ mHa is about three times too large, so the result is \emph{not}
chemically accurate. The threshold matters because reaction energies and barriers decide chemistry at the kcal/mol scale.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $3.14$ kcal/mol exceeds the 1 kcal/mol threshold.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.31$ multiplies by $62.751$ instead of $627.51$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $125.5$ multiplies by $25\,102$ (mixing units); $0.005\times627.51 = 3.14$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $1.6$ mHa $\approx 1$ kcal/mol is the target for useful chemistry.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{6}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Born--Oppenheimer; constant term}
In the Born--Oppenheimer approximation the nuclei are held fixed and only the electrons are treated quantum mechanically. In the
notebook's 4-qubit H$_2$ Hamiltonian, the nuclear--nuclear repulsion energy appears
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] nowhere, because nuclear repulsion is neglected in quantum chemistry
\item[\optlabel{B}] spread over the four $\texttt{XXYY}$-type exchange terms
\item[\optlabel{C}] as the coefficient of the $\texttt{ZZII}$ term
\item[\correctlabel{D}] inside the coefficient of the identity string $\texttt{IIII}$, as a constant energy shift
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} inside the coefficient of the identity string $\texttt{IIII}$, as a constant energy shift

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Born--Oppenheimer approximation; constants in a qubit Hamiltonian.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $V_{NN} = \sum_{A<B}\frac{Z_AZ_B}{R_{AB}}$ (atomic units); a constant $c$ maps to $c\,I^{\otimes n}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The molecular Hamiltonian is $H = T_e + V_{eN} + V_{ee} + V_{NN}$. With fixed nuclei (Born--Oppenheimer), $V_{NN} = \frac{Z_AZ_B}{R}$ is
just a number for a given bond length $R$. A number multiplies the identity operator, so after the fermion-to-qubit mapping it
ends up in the coefficient of $\texttt{IIII}$ (together with constant pieces of the electronic terms). The notebook's comment
says so: ``the constant term includes the nuclear repulsion energy''. It shifts every eigenvalue equally and needs no
measurement, but it must be included to compare with total energies such as the FCI value $-1.137284$ Ha.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $V_{NN}$ is included; otherwise total energies like $-1.137$ Ha could not be compared with experiment or FCI.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] The exchange terms describe the double excitation $\ket{1100} \leftrightarrow \ket{0011}$, not a constant.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $\texttt{ZZII}$ is an electron--electron interaction between spin-orbitals 0 and 1, not the nuclear repulsion.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Constants go into the identity coefficient: no measurement needed, but never forget them.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{7}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{Variational principle}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} For every normalised state $\ket\psi$, $\braket{\psi|H|\psi} \ge E_0$, where $E_0$ is the smallest eigenvalue of the
Hermitian operator $H$.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} Expanding $\ket\psi = \sum_k c_k\ket{E_k}$ in the orthonormal eigenbasis of $H$ gives $\braket{\psi|H|\psi} = \sum_k |c_k|^2E_k$ with
$\sum_k|c_k|^2 = 1$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Spectral theorem; variational principle.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\braket{\psi|H|\psi} = \sum_k|c_k|^2E_k \ge E_0$, $\sum|c_k|^2 = 1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{R is true:} a Hermitian $H$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis (spectral theorem). Then
$\braket{\psi|H|\psi} = \sum_{k,l} c_k^*c_l\braket{E_k|H|E_l} = \sum_{k,l}c_k^*c_lE_l\delta_{kl} = \sum_k|c_k|^2E_k$, and normalisation gives $\sum|c_k|^2 = 1$.
\textbf{A follows from R:} a weighted average with non-negative weights summing to 1 cannot be below the smallest value:
$\sum_k|c_k|^2E_k \ge \sum_k|c_k|^2E_0 = E_0$; equality iff all weight sits on ground states. R is the correct explanation. Answer: (A).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] needs A and R both true but R not explaining A; R is exactly the reason.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] needs A true and R false; R is true.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] needs A false and R true; A is true.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Energy expectation = weighted average of eigenvalues $\Rightarrow$ never below $E_0$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{8}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{Hermitian spectra}
\textbf{Statement I:} A real symmetric matrix can have complex (non-real) eigenvalues.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} Eigenvectors of a Hermitian matrix that belong to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\optlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\correctlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} Statement I is false, but Statement II is true

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Spectral properties of Hermitian matrices.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\lambda = v^\dagger Hv = \lambda^*$; $(\mu - \lambda)u^\dagger v = 0$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is false:} real symmetric matrices are Hermitian; if $Hv = \lambda v$ with $\|v\| = 1$ then
$\lambda = v^\dagger Hv = (v^\dagger Hv)^* = \lambda^*$, so $\lambda$ is real. (Complex eigenvalues occur for non-symmetric real matrices such as rotations.)
\textbf{II is true:} from $Hu = \lambda u$, $Hv = \mu v$: $\mu\,u^\dagger v = u^\dagger Hv = (Hu)^\dagger v = \lambda u^\dagger v$, so $(\mu - \lambda)u^\dagger v = 0$ and
$u^\dagger v = 0$ when $\lambda \neq \mu$. Real energies and orthogonal eigenstates are exactly what the variational argument uses. Answer: (D).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] needs both statements true; I is false.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] needs both statements false; II is true.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] needs I true and II false; I is false and II is true.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Hermitian $\Rightarrow$ real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{9}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Counting determinants}
H$_2$ in the STO-3G basis has 2 spatial orbitals, i.e.\ 4 spin-orbitals, and 2 electrons. The number of 2-electron Slater determinants,
and the number of them with one spin-up and one spin-down electron ($S_z = 0$), are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$6$ and $2$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$6$ and $4$ & \optlabel{C}\,$16$ and $4$ & \optlabel{D}\,$4$ and $2$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $6$ and $4$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Slater determinants as occupation patterns; spin sectors.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\#\text{det} = \binom{N_{\mathrm{so}}}{N_e}$; $S_z = 0$: $\binom{N_{\mathrm{orb}}}{N_\alpha}\binom{N_{\mathrm{orb}}}{N_\beta}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} A Slater determinant is fixed by choosing which spin-orbitals are occupied: $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ ways (the 4-qubit Fock space has $2^4 = 16$
basis states for \emph{all} electron numbers). With one $\alpha$ electron (2 choices of spatial orbital) and one $\beta$ electron (2 choices):
$2\times2 = 4$ determinants with $S_z = 0$. Exact diagonalisation within such a determinant space is \emph{full configuration
interaction} (FCI). The notebook's reference $-1.137284$ Ha is the FCI energy; its ground state uses only two of these
determinants, $\ket{1100}$ and $\ket{0011}$ (see Q.59).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $2$ counts only the closed-shell determinants ($\ket{1100}$, $\ket{0011}$).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $16 = 2^4$ counts all occupation patterns for any electron number.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $4$ would be $\binom41$ (one electron).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} FCI = exact diagonalisation within the fixed-electron-number determinant space.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{10}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{LiH qubit count}
LiH in the minimal STO-3G basis has one $1s$ orbital on H and the orbitals $1s, 2s, 2p_x, 2p_y, 2p_z$ on Li. With the Jordan--Wigner
mapping (one qubit per spin-orbital, no reductions), the number of qubits and the number of electrons are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$24$ qubits, $4$ electrons & \optlabel{B}\,$12$ qubits, $3$ electrons \\[3pt]
\correctlabel{C}\,$12$ qubits, $4$ electrons & \optlabel{D}\,$6$ qubits, $4$ electrons
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $12$ qubits, $4$ electrons

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Minimal basis; spin-orbitals; Jordan--Wigner qubit count.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} qubits $= 2\times$(spatial orbitals); electrons $=\sum Z_{\mathrm{atom}}$ (neutral).

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Spatial orbitals: $5$ (Li) $+ 1$ (H) $= 6$. Each holds a spin-up and a spin-down spin-orbital: $12$ spin-orbitals $\Rightarrow$ $12$
qubits under Jordan--Wigner. Electrons: Li has 3, H has 1: $4$. (Checked with PySCF in \texttt{verify\_answers.py}.) Freezing the Li $1s$
core and using symmetries reduces the qubit count further (Q.77). LiH is not part of the notebook; it is a standard
illustration of how molecular problems grow.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $24$ double-counts spin.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Li has 3 electrons and H one: 4, not 3.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $6$ counts spatial orbitals; each needs two qubits (spin up and down).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Count spatial orbitals, double for spin: LiH/STO-3G $\to$ 12 qubits.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{11}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Fermionic anticommutation}
Fermionic creation and annihilation operators $a_p^\dagger$, $a_p$ satisfy the canonical anticommutation relations. Match each expression
(List-I) with its value (List-II); $\ket{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the empty (vacuum) state.
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & $\{a_p, a_q^\dagger\} = a_pa_q^\dagger + a_q^\dagger a_p$ & \textbf{(1)} & $\{0, 1\}$ \\
\textbf{(Q)} & $a_p^\dagger a_p^\dagger$ & \textbf{(2)} & $\delta_{pq}\,I$ \\
\textbf{(R)} & spectrum of $n_p = a_p^\dagger a_p$ & \textbf{(3)} & $0$ (the zero vector) \\
\textbf{(S)} & $a_p\ket{\mathrm{vac}}$ & \textbf{(4)} & $0$ (the zero operator) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$4 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$3, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$1, S$\to$3
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Canonical anticommutation relations and their consequences.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\{a_p, a_q^\dagger\} = \delta_{pq}$, $\{a_p, a_q\} = 0$, $n_p^2 = n_p$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item P: canonical anticommutation relation $\{a_p, a_q^\dagger\} = \delta_{pq}I$ (2).
\item Q: $\{a_p^\dagger, a_p^\dagger\} = 2(a_p^\dagger)^2 = 0$, so $(a_p^\dagger)^2 = 0$ as an \emph{operator}: no orbital can be filled twice --- Pauli exclusion (4).
\item R: $n_p^2 = a_p^\dagger(a_pa_p^\dagger)a_p = a_p^\dagger(1 - a_p^\dagger a_p)a_p = n_p$, so $n_p$ is a projector with eigenvalues $0$ and $1$ (empty/occupied) (1).
\item S: there is nothing to remove from the vacuum: $a_p\ket{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the zero \emph{vector} (3).
\end{itemize}
These relations are what the Jordan--Wigner $Z$-strings must reproduce on qubits.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Q$\to$3, S$\to$4 confuses the zero operator $(a_p^\dagger)^2$ with the zero vector $a_p\ket{\mathrm{vac}}$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] R$\to$3, S$\to$1: the number operator has eigenvalues $\{0, 1\}$; annihilating the vacuum gives the zero vector.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] P$\to$4, Q$\to$2 swaps the CAR value with Pauli exclusion.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Fermions anticommute; qubit mappings must reproduce these signs.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{12}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{$O(N^4)$ Hamiltonian terms}
In second quantisation $H = \sum_{pq}h_{pq}a_p^\dagger a_q + \tfrac12\sum_{pqrs}h_{pqrs}a_p^\dagger a_q^\dagger a_ra_s$ (+ constant). For $N$ spin-orbitals the number of
terms in this Hamiltonian grows as
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] $O(N)$, one term per orbital
\item[\correctlabel{B}] $O(N^4)$, from the two-electron integrals $h_{pqrs}$
\item[\optlabel{C}] $O(N^2)$, from the one-electron integrals only
\item[\optlabel{D}] $O(2^N)$, like the dimension of the Fock space
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $O(N^4)$, from the two-electron integrals $h_{pqrs}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Second-quantised Hamiltonian; number of integrals.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} one-body $h_{pq}$: $N^2$; two-body $h_{pqrs}$: $N^4$ (reduced $\approx 8\times$ by symmetry).

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The one-body part has $N^2$ coefficients $h_{pq}$, the two-body part $N^4$ coefficients $h_{pqrs}$ (four free indices). Permutation symmetries
reduce the count by a constant factor (about 8) but not the power, so the total is $O(N^4)$. After a fermion-to-qubit mapping each
term becomes a few Pauli strings, so the number of Pauli terms --- and the measurement cost of VQE --- also grows like $N^4$.
The Hilbert space is $2^N$-dimensional, but the Hamiltonian itself has only polynomially many terms; that is what makes
$\braket{H} = \sum_kc_k\braket{P_k}$ practical. H$_2$ (STO-3G): 15 Pauli terms.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $O(N)$ would mean no interactions between orbitals.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $O(N^2)$ ignores the two-electron integrals, which dominate.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $2^N$ is the state-space dimension, not the number of terms.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Polynomially many terms make $\braket H = \sum c_k\braket{P_k}$ feasible; $N^4$ still makes measurement costly.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{13}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{$e^{i\theta P}$ identity}
For a Pauli operator $P$ ($P^2 = I$), $e^{i\theta P} = \cos\theta\,I + i\sin\theta\,P$. Hence $e^{i\pi X/4}$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\begin{pmatrix}0 & i\\ i & 0\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & i\\ i & 1\end{pmatrix}$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & -i\\ -i & 1\end{pmatrix}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & i\\ i & 1\end{pmatrix}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Exponential of an involutory matrix.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $e^{i\theta P} = \cos\theta\,I + i\sin\theta\,P$ for $P^2 = I$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Power series: even powers of $P$ give $I$, odd powers give $P$, so $e^{i\theta P} = \sum_k\frac{(i\theta)^k}{k!}P^k = \cos\theta\,I + i\sin\theta\,P$.
With $\theta = \pi/4$: $\cos\frac\pi4 = \sin\frac\pi4 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $e^{i\pi X/4} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(I + iX) = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{psmallmatrix}1 & i\\ i & 1\end{psmallmatrix}$.
The same identity, with $P = X_0X_1X_2Y_3$, is how CUDA-Q's \texttt{exp\_pauli(theta, q, "XXXY")} acts in the notebook's UCC ansatz.
$\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(I - iX)$ would be $e^{-i\pi X/4} = R_X(\pi/2)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $iX = e^{i\pi X/2}$, a quarter period further.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] That is the Hadamard gate, not an $X$ rotation.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(I - iX)$ is $e^{-i\pi X/4}$ (opposite sign).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Same identity powers \texttt{exp\_pauli}: $e^{i\theta P} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta P$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 14 and 15}
A single qubit has the Hamiltonian $H = -Z + \tfrac12 X = \begin{pmatrix}-1 & \tfrac12\\ \tfrac12 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.
A one-parameter trial state is prepared as $\ket{\psi(\theta)} = R_Y(\theta)\ket0 = \cos\tfrac\theta2\ket0 + \sin\tfrac\theta2\ket1$, and its
energy $E(\theta) = \braket{\psi(\theta)|H|\psi(\theta)}$ is minimised over $\theta \in (-\pi, \pi]$.
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{14}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{One-qubit $E(\theta)$ and $E_0$}
The energy function $E(\theta)$ and the exact ground-state energy $E_0$ are
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] $E(\theta) = -\cos\theta + \tfrac12\sin\theta$ and $E_0 = -1$
\item[\optlabel{B}] $E(\theta) = -\cos\tfrac\theta2 + \tfrac12\sin\tfrac\theta2$ and $E_0 = -\tfrac{\sqrt5}{2}$
\item[\optlabel{C}] $E(\theta) = -\cos\theta + \sin\theta$ and $E_0 = -\sqrt2$
\item[\correctlabel{D}] $E(\theta) = -\cos\theta + \tfrac12\sin\theta$ and $E_0 = -\tfrac{\sqrt5}{2} \approx -1.118$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $E(\theta) = -\cos\theta + \tfrac12\sin\theta$ and $E_0 = -\tfrac{\sqrt5}{2} \approx -1.118$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Expectation values of a parameterised qubit; diagonalising a $2\times2$ Hamiltonian.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $R_Y(\theta)\ket0$: $\braket Z = \cos\theta$, $\braket X = \sin\theta$; $\lambda = \pm\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ for $aZ + bX$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} For $\ket\psi = \cos\frac\theta2\ket0 + \sin\frac\theta2\ket1$: $\braket Z = \cos^2\frac\theta2 - \sin^2\frac\theta2 = \cos\theta$ and
$\braket X = 2\cos\frac\theta2\sin\frac\theta2 = \sin\theta$. By linearity $E(\theta) = -\braket Z + \tfrac12\braket X = -\cos\theta + \tfrac12\sin\theta$.
Eigenvalues of $\begin{psmallmatrix}-1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{psmallmatrix}$: $\lambda^2 - 1 - \tfrac14 = 0$, $\lambda = \pm\sqrt{5/4} = \pm\frac{\sqrt5}{2}$, so $E_0 = -1.1180$.
Consistency: $E(\theta) = -\sqrt{1 + \tfrac14}\cos(\theta + \varphi)$ has minimum $-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}$ --- the one-parameter $R_Y$ ansatz reaches $E_0$ exactly,
because the ground state of a real $2\times2$ Hamiltonian is a real vector.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $-1$ is $E(0) = \braket{0|H|0}$, the diagonal element, not the minimum.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Half angles appear in the amplitudes, not in the expectation values.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The $X$ coefficient is $\frac12$, not $1$; $-\sqrt2$ belongs to $-Z + X$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} For $aZ + bX$: $E_0 = -\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, reachable with one $R_Y$ angle.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{15}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Optimal angle, starting error}
The optimal angle $\theta^*$, and the energy error $E(0) - E_0$ of the starting point $\theta = 0$ (the state $\ket0$), are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\theta^* = -\arctan\tfrac12 \approx -0.464$ rad; error $0$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\theta^* = -\arctan 2 \approx -1.107$ rad; error $\approx 0.118$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$\theta^* = +\arctan\tfrac12 \approx 0.464$ rad; error $\approx 0.118$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$\theta^* = -\arctan\tfrac12 \approx -0.464$ rad; error $\approx 0.118$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $\theta^* = -\arctan\tfrac12 \approx -0.464$ rad; error $\approx 0.118$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Stationary points; second-derivative test.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E'(\theta) = \sin\theta + \frac12\cos\theta$; $\tan\theta^* = -\frac12$; $E'' > 0$ at a minimum.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $E'(\theta) = \sin\theta + \tfrac12\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \tan\theta = -\tfrac12$. The minimum needs $E'' = \cos\theta - \tfrac12\sin\theta > 0$: with
$\theta^* = -\arctan\tfrac12 = -0.4636$, $\cos\theta^* = 0.894 > 0$ and $\sin\theta^* = -0.447$, so $E'' > 0$ and
$E(\theta^*) = -0.894 - 0.224 = -1.118 = E_0$. (The other root $\pi - 0.4636$ is the maximum $+1.118$.)
$E(0) = -1$, so the starting error is $-1 - (-1.118) = 0.118$. The negative angle mixes in $\ket1$ with a \emph{negative} amplitude because the
off-diagonal element $+\tfrac12$ is positive.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] The start $\ket0$ is not the ground state, so its error is not zero.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\arctan2$ inverts the ratio; $E(-1.107) = -0.447 - 0.447 = -0.894$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $+0.464$ has the wrong sign: there $E = -0.894 + 0.224 = -0.671$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Off-diagonal sign decides the sign of the optimal mixing angle.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{16}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Pauli decomposition ($2\times2$)}
The Hermitian matrix $M = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 - 2i\\ 1 + 2i & -1\end{pmatrix}$ written as $aI + bX + cY + dZ$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$I + X + 2Y + 2Z$ & \optlabel{B}\,$3I + X + 2Y - Z$ & \optlabel{C}\,$I + X - 2Y + 2Z$ & \optlabel{D}\,$2I + X + 2Y + Z$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $I + X + 2Y + 2Z$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Pauli decomposition of a Hermitian matrix.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $M = \sum_P c_PP$, $c_P = \frac12\operatorname{tr}(PM)$; $M_{01} = b - ic$, $M_{00} = a + d$, $M_{11} = a - d$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Use $c_P = \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(PM)$ (Paulis are orthogonal: $\operatorname{tr}(PQ) = 2\delta_{PQ}$).
$a = \tfrac12(3 - 1) = 1$; $d = \tfrac12(3 + 1) = 2$; $b = \tfrac12(M_{01} + M_{10}) = \tfrac12\cdot2 = 1$; $c = \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(YM) = \tfrac12(-iM_{10} + iM_{01}) = \tfrac12(-i(1 + 2i) + i(1 - 2i)) = \tfrac12(2 + 2) = 2$.
Check: $X + 2Y = \begin{psmallmatrix}0 & 1 - 2i\\ 1 + 2i & 0\end{psmallmatrix}$ \checkmark{} and $I + 2Z = \operatorname{diag}(3, -1)$ \checkmark{}. Real coefficients are guaranteed because $M$ is Hermitian --- the
reason the notebook rejects complex coefficients in \texttt{CUSTOM\_HAMILTONIAN}.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $3I - Z$ gives diagonal $(2, 4)$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $-2Y$ gives $M_{01} = 1 + 2i$, the conjugate of the given entry.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $2I + Z$ gives diagonal $(3, 1)$, not $(3, -1)$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Real coefficients for every Pauli string $\iff$ Hermitian matrix.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{17}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Pauli decomposition (diagonal)}
The diagonal two-qubit Hamiltonian $H = \operatorname{diag}(1, 2, 3, 4)$ (basis $\ket{00}, \ket{01}, \ket{10}, \ket{11}$) written as a sum of Pauli strings is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$2.5\,II - 0.5\,ZI - 1.0\,IZ$ & \optlabel{B}\,$2.5\,II - 1.0\,ZI - 0.5\,IZ + 0.5\,ZZ$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$2.5\,II + 1.0\,ZI + 0.5\,IZ$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$2.5\,II - 1.0\,ZI - 0.5\,IZ$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $2.5\,II - 1.0\,ZI - 0.5\,IZ$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Pauli decomposition of diagonal operators.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $c_P = 2^{-n}\operatorname{tr}(PH)$; $ZI = \operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1,-1)$, $IZ = \operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,-1)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Coefficients $c_P = \tfrac14\operatorname{tr}(PH)$. On the basis states, $ZI = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -1, -1)$, $IZ = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 1, -1)$, $ZZ = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, 1)$.
$c_{II} = \frac{1+2+3+4}{4} = 2.5$; $c_{ZI} = \frac{1+2-3-4}{4} = -1$; $c_{IZ} = \frac{1-2+3-4}{4} = -0.5$; $c_{ZZ} = \frac{1-2-3+4}{4} = 0$.
Check $\ket{11}$: $2.5 + 1 + 0.5 = 4$ \checkmark{}. The first qubit (more significant) changes the energy by 2, so its $Z$ coefficient is $-1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Swaps the two qubits' roles; the first qubit changes the energy by 2, the second by 1.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $c_{ZZ} = \frac{1 - 2 - 3 + 4}{4} = 0$: the levels are additive, no interaction term.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Positive $Z$ coefficients would make $\ket{00}$ the highest level; it is the lowest ($1$).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Diagonal Hamiltonians need only $I$/$Z$ strings.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{18}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{RHF at dissociation}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} For H$_2$ at large bond length, the restricted Hartree--Fock (single closed-shell determinant) energy lies far above
the exact energy.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} The nuclear--nuclear repulsion $1/R$ tends to zero as $R \to \infty$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\correctlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Static correlation; RHF failure at dissociation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\sigma_g^2 \propto (1s_Q.1s_B + 1s_Q.21s_A) + (1s_A^2 + 1s_B^2)$: $50\,\%$ ionic.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{A is true:} the RHF determinant puts both electrons in the bonding orbital $\sigma_g = (1s_A + 1s_B)/\sqrt2$. Expanded in atomic
orbitals it contains ionic configurations (H$^+$H$^-$) with $50\,\%$ weight, which cost a lot of energy for separated atoms. The exact
state is $\approx \cos\theta\ket{\sigma_g^2} - \sin\theta\ket{\sigma_u^2}$ with $\theta \to \pi/4$: static correlation. (Same structure as the notebook's UCC
state $\cos\theta\ket{1100} - \sin\theta\ket{0011}$.)
\textbf{R is true} but is \emph{not} the explanation: $V_{NN}$ is identical in RHF and the exact calculation and cancels in the error. Answer: (B).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] needs A true, R true \emph{and} R explaining A; $V_{NN}$ is the same in both methods and cannot explain the error.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] needs A true and R false; R is true.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] needs A false and R true; A is true.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Bond breaking needs more than one determinant --- VQE's double excitation provides it.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{19}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Correlation energy}
For the notebook's H$_2$ Hamiltonian, the Hartree--Fock energy is $E_{\mathrm{HF}} = \braket{1100|H|1100} = -1.116759$ Ha and the FCI energy is
$-1.137284$ Ha. The correlation energy $E_{\mathrm{corr}} = E_{\mathrm{FCI}} - E_{\mathrm{HF}}$ is about
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$-20.5$ mHa & \optlabel{B}\,$+20.5$ mHa & \optlabel{C}\,$-2.05$ mHa & \optlabel{D}\,$-1137$ mHa
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $-20.5$ mHa

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Correlation energy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E_{\mathrm{corr}} = E_{\mathrm{FCI}} - E_{\mathrm{HF}} \le 0$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $E_{\mathrm{corr}} = -1.137284 - (-1.116759) = -0.020525$ Ha $= -20.5$ mHa. It is negative because FCI is variationally
\emph{lower} than HF (HF is one particular state in the same space). $20.5$ mHa $\approx 12.9$ kcal/mol, far above chemical accuracy:
HF alone is not good enough, and VQE has to recover this correlation energy. The UCC parameter does exactly that (see Q.59--Q.60).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Positive sign would mean FCI is above HF, violating the variational principle.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Off by a factor of 10: $-0.020525$ Ha is $-20.5$ mHa, not $-2.05$ mHa.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $-1137$ mHa is the total FCI energy.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} H$_2$: $20.5$ mHa of correlation, about $13\times$ chemical accuracy.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{20}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Excited-state contamination}
A trial state of H$_2$ has $90\,\%$ weight on the ground state ($E_0 = -1.13728$ Ha) and $10\,\%$ on another eigenstate of the 4-qubit Hamiltonian with energy
$E_1 = -0.53821$ Ha. Its energy expectation and its error above $E_0$ are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$-1.1971$ Ha and $-59.9$ mHa & \correctlabel{B}\,$-1.0774$ Ha and $59.9$ mHa \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$-0.8378$ Ha and $299.5$ mHa & \optlabel{D}\,$-1.1373$ Ha and $0$ mHa
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $-1.0774$ Ha and $59.9$ mHa

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Energy of a state expanded in eigenstates.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E = \sum|c_k|^2E_k$; error $= \sum_{k>0}|c_k|^2(E_k - E_0)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $E = \sum_k|c_k|^2E_k = 0.9(-1.13728) + 0.1(-0.53821) = -1.02355 - 0.05382 = -1.07738$ Ha.
Error $E - E_0 = 0.1(E_1 - E_0) = 0.1\times0.59907 = 0.0599$ Ha $= 59.9$ mHa. The error is \emph{linear} in the contaminating weight and is
always non-negative (variational principle). The energy is lower than the energies of all excited states but still above $E_0$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Below $E_0$: impossible for a normalised state.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Uses $50\,\%$ weight instead of $10\,\%$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Ignores the $10\,\%$ excited weight.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Energy errors are linear in contamination; state errors are larger than they look.
\end{solbox}
\qsep
