\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{21}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{$R_Y$ and the Born rule}
The state $R_Y(\pi/3)\ket0$ is measured in the computational basis. The probability of the outcome 1 is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\tfrac34$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ & \optlabel{C}\,$\tfrac12$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$\tfrac14$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $\tfrac14$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} $R_Y$ rotation and the Born rule.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $R_Y(\theta)\ket0 = \cos\frac\theta2\ket0 + \sin\frac\theta2\ket1$; $P(1) = \sin^2\frac\theta2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $R_Y(\theta) = e^{-i\theta Y/2} = \begin{psmallmatrix}\cos\frac\theta2 & -\sin\frac\theta2\\ \sin\frac\theta2 & \cos\frac\theta2\end{psmallmatrix}$, so $R_Y(\theta)\ket0 = \cos\frac\theta2\ket0 + \sin\frac\theta2\ket1$
(real amplitudes). With $\theta = \pi/3$: $P(1) = \sin^2(\pi/6) = \tfrac14$, $P(0) = \cos^2(\pi/6) = \tfrac34$. The notebook's hardware-efficient
ansatz is built from exactly these \texttt{ry} rotations.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $\frac34 = \cos^2(\pi/6)$ is $P(0)$, the probability of the \emph{other} outcome.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \cos(\pi/6)$ is the \emph{amplitude} of $\ket0$; probabilities are squared moduli ($P(1) = \sin^2(\pi/6) = \frac14$).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $\frac12$ needs $\theta = \pi/2$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Half angles in amplitudes: $R_Y(\theta)$ rotates the Bloch vector by $\theta$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{22}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Pauli products}
The two-qubit operator $(X\otimes Y)(Y\otimes X)$ equals
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$Z\otimes Z$ & \optlabel{B}\,$Y\otimes Y$ & \optlabel{C}\,$-Z\otimes Z$ & \optlabel{D}\,$i\,Z\otimes Z$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $Z\otimes Z$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Pauli multiplication; tensor products.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $XY = iZ$, $YX = -iZ$; $(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D) = AC\otimes BD$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Multiply factor-wise: $(X\otimes Y)(Y\otimes X) = (XY)\otimes(YX)$. Pauli table: $XY = iZ$, $YX = -iZ$. So the product is
$(iZ)\otimes(-iZ) = -i^2\,Z\otimes Z = Z\otimes Z$. Products of Pauli strings are again Pauli strings up to a phase $\pm1, \pm i$ --- the
algebra behind Hamiltonian decompositions such as the notebook's $\texttt{XXYY}$, $\texttt{XYYX}$, \dots\ terms.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $Y\otimes Y$ ignores the products.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $-Z\otimes Z$ uses $YX = +iZ$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Keeps a phase $i$; the two phases $i$ and $-i$ multiply to $1$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Track the phases $\pm i$ factor by factor.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{23}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Bloch vectors}
Match each single-qubit state (List-I) with its Bloch vector $(\braket X, \braket Y, \braket Z)$ (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & $\ket0$ & \textbf{(1)} & $(0, 1, 0)$ \\
\textbf{(Q)} & $\ket- = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 - \ket1)$ & \textbf{(2)} & $(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, 0, \tfrac12)$ \\
\textbf{(R)} & $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + i\ket1)$ & \textbf{(3)} & $(0, 0, 1)$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & $R_Y(\pi/3)\ket0$ & \textbf{(4)} & $(-1, 0, 0)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$2 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \correctlabel{D}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Bloch vector of a qubit state.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $(\braket X, \braket Y, \braket Z) = (2\mathrm{Re}\,a^*b, 2\mathrm{Im}\,a^*b, |a|^2 - |b|^2)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} For $\ket\psi = a\ket0 + b\ket1$: $\braket Z = |a|^2 - |b|^2$, $\braket X = 2\,\mathrm{Re}(a^*b)$, $\braket Y = 2\,\mathrm{Im}(a^*b)$.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item P: $a = 1$, $b = 0$: $(0, 0, 1)$ (3).
\item Q: $a = -b = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$: $\braket X = -1$: $(-1, 0, 0)$ (4).
\item R: $a^*b = \frac i2$: $\braket Y = 1$: $(0, 1, 0)$ (1).
\item S: $R_Y(\theta)\ket0$ has Bloch vector $(\sin\theta, 0, \cos\theta)$; $\theta = \pi/3$: $(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}, 0, \frac12)$ (2). $R_Y$ rotates in the $x$--$z$ plane:
real amplitudes, $\braket Y = 0$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] R$\to$2, S$\to$1 gives $\ket{+i}$ a real Bloch vector; $R_Y$ never creates $\braket Y \neq 0$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Q$\to$1, R$\to$4 swaps $\ket-$ and $\ket{+i}$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] P$\to$4 would put $\ket0$ on the $-x$ axis.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $R_Y$ keeps states in the real $x$--$z$ plane.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{24}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Measurement basis changes}
To estimate $\braket P$ from computational-basis measurements, each Pauli string is first rotated into a string of $Z$'s and $I$'s. Match each
observable (List-I) with the gates applied before measuring (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & $X$ & \textbf{(1)} & $H$ on qubit 0 only \\
\textbf{(Q)} & $Y$ & \textbf{(2)} & nothing \\
\textbf{(R)} & $Z$ & \textbf{(3)} & $H$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & $X_0Z_1$ & \textbf{(4)} & $S^\dagger$, then $H$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$2, R$\to$4, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 \\[3pt]
\correctlabel{C}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$2, S$\to$1
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Measurement basis changes.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $HXH = Z$; $(HS^\dagger)Y(HS^\dagger)^\dagger = Z$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} If $UPU^\dagger = Z$, measuring $Z$ after applying $U$ gives the eigenvalues of $P$: $\braket{\psi|P|\psi} = \braket{U\psi|Z|U\psi}$.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item P: $HXH = Z$: apply $H$ (3).
\item Q: $(HS^\dagger)\,Y\,(HS^\dagger)^\dagger = Z$: apply $S^\dagger$ first, then $H$ (4) (checked numerically in \texttt{verify\_answers.py}).
\item R: $Z$ is already diagonal: nothing (2).
\item S: rotate only the $X$ factor: $H$ on qubit 0; then $\braket{X_0Z_1}$ is the average of $(-1)^{b_0\oplus b_1}$ (1).
\end{itemize}
The notebook's text describes the same rule (``$H$ for $X$, $S^\dagger H$ for $Y$''); \texttt{cudaq.observe} does it automatically with shots.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Q$\to$2 means measuring $Y$ without a basis change, which measures $Z$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] R$\to$1, S$\to$2: $Z$ needs nothing, but $X_0Z_1$ needs $H$ on qubit 0.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] P$\to$4, Q$\to$3 swaps the $X$ and $Y$ rotations.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Rotate each Pauli factor to $Z$, then multiply the $\pm1$ outcomes.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{25}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Bell-state correlations}
For the Bell state $\ket{\Phi^+} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} + \ket{11})$, the expectation value $\braket{Y\otimes Y}$ is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$+1$ & \optlabel{B}\,$-\tfrac12$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$-1$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $-1$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Action of $Y$; Bell-state correlations.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $Y\ket0 = i\ket1$, $Y\ket1 = -i\ket0$; $\ket{\Phi^+}$: $\braket{XX} = \braket{ZZ} = 1$, $\braket{YY} = -1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $Y\ket0 = i\ket1$, $Y\ket1 = -i\ket0$. So $(Y\otimes Y)\ket{00} = i\cdot i\ket{11} = -\ket{11}$ and $(Y\otimes Y)\ket{11} = (-i)(-i)\ket{00} = -\ket{00}$:
$(Y\otimes Y)\ket{\Phi^+} = -\ket{\Phi^+}$, an eigenstate with eigenvalue $-1$. (Consistency: $\braket{XX} = 1$, $\braket{ZZ} = 1$ and
$XX\cdot YY\cdot ZZ$-relation $(X\otimes X)(Y\otimes Y) = -(Z\otimes Z)$ gives $1\cdot\braket{YY} = -1$.)

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Forgets $i\cdot i = -1$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Expectation values of eigenstates are eigenvalues: $\pm1$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The state is an eigenstate of $Y\otimes Y$, so the value is $\pm1$, not $0$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $\ket{\Phi^+}$ is a joint eigenstate of $XX$, $YY$, $ZZ$ with eigenvalues $(1, -1, 1)$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{26}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Qubit ordering in CUDA-Q}
The Hartree--Fock state of the notebook's H$_2$ example is $\ket{1100}$, written with qubit 0 first. In the vector returned by \texttt{cudaq.get\_state},
which lists amplitudes with qubit 0 as the \emph{least} significant bit, this basis state has the index
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$12$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$3$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0$ & \optlabel{D}\,$6$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $3$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Qubit ordering conventions.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} little-endian index $= \sum_kq_k2^k$; big-endian $= \sum_kq_k2^{n-1-k}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Qubit 0 first means the string $q_0q_1q_2q_3 = 1100$. With qubit 0 as the least significant bit the index is
$\sum_k q_k2^k = 1\cdot1 + 1\cdot2 + 0\cdot4 + 0\cdot8 = 3$. Read as a big-endian number the same string would be $12$. Mixing up the two
orderings is a classic source of wrong amplitudes; the repository's lecture scripts reorder CUDA-Q state vectors before comparing them
with NumPy for exactly this reason.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $12$ reads the string big-endian (qubit 0 most significant).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Index $0$ is the all-zero state $\ket{0000}$, the empty (vacuum) occupation, not Hartree--Fock.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $6 = 0110_2$ has the wrong bits set.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Always state the bit order; CUDA-Q state vectors are little-endian.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{27}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Entangling with CNOT}
Starting from $\ket{00}$, apply $R_Y(\pi/2)$ to qubit 0 and then a CNOT with control 0 and target 1. The resulting state is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} + \ket{11})$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} + \ket{10})$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} - \ket{11})$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\tfrac12(\ket{00} + \ket{01} + \ket{10} + \ket{11})$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} + \ket{11})$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Entangling with CNOT.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathrm{CNOT}\ket{a, b} = \ket{a, a\oplus b}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $R_Y(\pi/2)\ket0 = \cos\frac\pi4\ket0 + \sin\frac\pi4\ket1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket0 + \ket1)$, so after the first gate $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} + \ket{10})$.
The CNOT flips qubit 1 when qubit 0 is 1: $\ket{10} \to \ket{11}$. Result: the Bell state $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} + \ket{11})$ --- entangled. This is
how the CNOT ladder of the hardware-efficient ansatz creates entanglement between neighbouring qubits.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] That is the state before the CNOT.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $R_Y(\pi/2)$ gives a $+$ sign: $\sin\frac\pi4 > 0$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Needs a rotation on qubit 1 as well.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $R_Y$ + CNOT ladder = the entangling backbone of the hardware-efficient ansatz.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{28}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{Normalisation; measuring $X$}
\textbf{Statement I:} Any circuit of gates applied to $\ket{0\dots0}$ prepares a normalised state, so the ansatz state $\ket{\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)}$ needs no
explicit normalisation.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} Measuring in the computational basis directly reveals the eigenvalue of an $X_i$ term, without any basis change.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\correctlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} Statement I is true, but Statement II is false

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Unitarity preserves norm; measurement bases.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\|U\ket\psi\| = \|\ket\psi\|$; measure $X$ via $H$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is true:} gates are unitary, $\|U\ket\psi\| = \|\ket\psi\|$, so $\ket{\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)} = U(\boldsymbol\theta)\ket{0\dots0}$ has norm 1 for every $\boldsymbol\theta$. This is why
VQE can use $\braket{\psi|H|\psi}$ directly, without dividing by $\braket{\psi|\psi}$ as in a Rayleigh quotient.
\textbf{II is false:} a $Z$-basis measurement yields eigenvalues of $Z$; for $X_i$ a Hadamard on qubit $i$ is needed first (Q.24). Answer: (C).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] needs both statements true; II is false.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] needs both statements false; I is true.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] needs I false and II true; I is true, II false.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Circuit states are automatically normalised; non-$Z$ terms need basis changes.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{29}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Commuting vs.\ qubit-wise commuting}
Consider the four exchange terms of the notebook's H$_2$ Hamiltonian, $\texttt{XXYY}$, $\texttt{XYYX}$, $\texttt{YXXY}$, $\texttt{YYXX}$. Which statement is
correct?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Every pair anticommutes
\item[\correctlabel{B}] All six pairs commute, but no pair is qubit-wise commuting
\item[\optlabel{C}] Only $\texttt{XXYY}$ and $\texttt{YYXX}$ commute
\item[\optlabel{D}] All six pairs are qubit-wise commuting, so one measurement setting suffices
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} All six pairs commute, but no pair is qubit-wise commuting

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} General versus qubit-wise commutation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} commute $\iff$ even number of anticommuting positions; QWC $\iff$ each position equal or $I$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Two Pauli strings commute iff they differ by anticommuting single-qubit factors at an \emph{even} number of positions.
$\texttt{XXYY}$ vs $\texttt{XYYX}$: positions 1 and 3 differ ($X$/$Y$) --- two: commute. $\texttt{XXYY}$ vs $\texttt{YXXY}$: positions 0 and 2 --- commute.
$\texttt{XXYY}$ vs $\texttt{YYXX}$: all four positions --- commute. Likewise for the remaining three pairs.
\emph{Qubit-wise} commuting requires, at every position, equal letters or an $I$; every pair here has positions with $X$ against $Y$, so
no pair qualifies. Consequence: with simple qubit-wise grouping these 4 terms need 4 settings; with general commuting grouping (a
joint basis change containing CNOTs) they need only one (Q.54).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Each pair differs at an even number of positions, so they commute.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] All six pairs commute, not only one.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] No pair is QWC: every pair has positions with $X$ against $Y$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Commuting $\ne$ qubit-wise commuting; the difference costs measurement settings.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{30}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{\texttt{exp\_pauli} on eigenstates}
CUDA-Q's \texttt{exp\_pauli(theta, q, word)} applies $e^{i\theta P}$ for the Pauli string $P$ given by \texttt{word}. Applied with the word
$\texttt{"ZZ"}$ to the basis state $\ket{01}$, it gives
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\cos\theta\ket{01} + i\sin\theta\ket{10}$ & \optlabel{B}\,$e^{+i\theta}\ket{01}$ \\[3pt]
\correctlabel{C}\,$e^{-i\theta}\ket{01}$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\ket{10}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $e^{-i\theta}\ket{01}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Exponential of a Pauli string on its eigenstate.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $P\ket v = \lambda\ket v \Rightarrow e^{i\theta P}\ket v = e^{i\theta\lambda}\ket v$; $ZZ\ket{01} = -\ket{01}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $Z\otimes Z\ket{01} = (+1)(-1)\ket{01} = -\ket{01}$: an eigenstate with eigenvalue $-1$. On an eigenvector, $e^{i\theta P}$ acts as the number
$e^{i\theta\lambda} = e^{-i\theta}$. A diagonal Pauli string only adds phases; it never changes bit values. The sign convention ($e^{+i\theta P}$,
verified with CUDA-Q 0.16) matters for the notebook's UCC state $\cos\theta\ket{1100} - \sin\theta\ket{0011}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] A diagonal string cannot change bits.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Uses eigenvalue $+1$; $\ket{01}$ has different bits.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Bit flips need $X$/$Y$ factors.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Diagonal Pauli exponentials only add phases.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{31}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{$\texttt{XXXY}\ket{1100}$}
The four-qubit Pauli string $X_0X_1X_2Y_3$ (word $\texttt{"XXXY"}$) acting on $\ket{1100}$ gives
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$i\ket{0011}$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\ket{0011}$ & \optlabel{C}\,$-i\ket{0011}$ & \optlabel{D}\,$i\ket{1100}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $i\ket{0011}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Pauli strings on basis states.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $X\ket b = \ket{1-b}$; $Y\ket0 = i\ket1$, $Y\ket1 = -i\ket0$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Qubit by qubit: $X\ket1 = \ket0$ (qubits 0, 1), $X\ket0 = \ket1$ (qubit 2), $Y\ket0 = i\ket1$ (qubit 3). Product: $i\ket{0011}$.
Hence $e^{i\theta P}\ket{1100} = \cos\theta\ket{1100} + i\sin\theta\,(i\ket{0011}) = \cos\theta\ket{1100} - \sin\theta\ket{0011}$: the notebook's
UCC state. The single Pauli string moves both electrons from orbital 0 (qubits 0, 1) to orbital 1 (qubits 2, 3) --- a double excitation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Drops the factor $i$ from $Y$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $-i$ comes from $Y\ket1$, but qubit 3 is in $\ket0$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $X$ flips bits; the state changes.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $\texttt{XXXY}$ moves both electrons from orbital 0 to orbital 1.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{32}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{Real expectation values}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} For a Hermitian $H$, the expectation value $\braket{\psi|H|\psi}$ is a real number for every state $\ket\psi$.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} The identity $\braket{\psi|H|\psi} = \braket{\psi|H|\psi}^*$ holds only for normalised states.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\correctlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} A is true, but R is false

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Hermiticity implies real expectation values.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\braket{\psi|H|\psi}^* = \braket{\psi|H^\dagger|\psi} = \braket{\psi|H|\psi}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{A is true:} $\braket{\psi|H|\psi}^* = \braket{\psi|H^\dagger|\psi} = \braket{\psi|H|\psi}$, so it equals its own complex conjugate.
\textbf{R is false:} the identity uses only $H = H^\dagger$; it holds for every vector, normalised or not (the norm $\braket{\psi|\psi}$ is real anyway).
Real energies are why a VQE energy can be compared with $E_0$ at all. Answer: (C).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] needs A true, R true \emph{and} R explaining A; R is false.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] needs A and R both true but R not explaining A; R is false.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] needs A false and R true; A is true, R false.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Real energies need only $H = H^\dagger$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{33}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{State-vector / density-matrix memory}
A complex fp64 amplitude needs 16 bytes. For LiH in STO-3G with Jordan--Wigner (12 qubits), the memory needed for the state vector and
for the density matrix ($2^n\times2^n$ amplitudes) is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$192$ B and $2.3$ kB & \optlabel{B}\,$65.5$ kB and $131$ kB \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$268$ MB and $65.5$ kB & \correctlabel{D}\,$65.5$ kB and $268$ MB
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $65.5$ kB and $268$ MB

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Memory of state vectors and density matrices.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} state: $16\cdot2^n$ B; density matrix: $16\cdot4^n$ B.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} State vector: $16\times2^{12} = 16\times4096 = 65\,536$ bytes $\approx 65.5$ kB. Density matrix: $16\times4^{12} = 16\times16\,777\,216 = 268\,435\,456$ bytes
$\approx 268$ MB. Density matrices (needed for exact noisy simulation, target \texttt{density-matrix-cpu}) square the cost; at the notebook's 15
qubits the density matrix would need $17.2$ GB versus $524$ kB for the state vector.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $192 = 16\times12$ treats memory as linear in $n$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $131$ kB is twice the state vector, not $4^n$ scaling.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Swaps the two values.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Noisy (density-matrix) simulation squares the memory.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{34}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{$\braket{Z_0Z_1}$ through a CNOT}
Two qubits start in $\ket{00}$; $R_Y(\theta_0)$ and $R_Y(\theta_1)$ are applied to qubits 0 and 1, followed by a CNOT (control 0, target 1). The
expectation value $\braket{Z_0Z_1}$ of the final state is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\cos(\theta_0 + \theta_1)$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$\cos\theta_1$ & \optlabel{C}\,$\cos\theta_0$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\cos\theta_0\cos\theta_1$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $\cos\theta_1$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Heisenberg picture through a CNOT.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathrm{CNOT}\,Z_0Z_1\,\mathrm{CNOT} = Z_1$; $\braket{Z}_{R_Y(\theta)\ket0} = \cos\theta$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Heisenberg picture: $\braket{Z_0Z_1}_{\text{after}} = \braket{\mathrm{CNOT}\,Z_0Z_1\,\mathrm{CNOT}}_{\text{before}}$. CNOT conjugation maps $Z_1 \to Z_0Z_1$, hence
$Z_0Z_1 \to Z_0\cdot Z_0Z_1 = Z_1$. So $\braket{Z_0Z_1}_{\text{after}} = \braket{Z_1}_{\text{before}} = \cos\theta_1$ (Bloch vector of $R_Y(\theta_1)\ket0$).
Direct check with the bits: after the CNOT, $z_1' = z_0\oplus z_1$, so $z_0 \oplus z_1' = z_1$ and $(-1)^{z_0\oplus z_1'} = (-1)^{z_1}$. Before the CNOT the
answer would have been $\cos\theta_0\cos\theta_1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Expectation values of product states multiply; they do not add angles.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $Z_0Z_1$ maps to $Z_1$, not $Z_0$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $\cos\theta_0\cos\theta_1$ is the value \emph{before} the CNOT.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Propagate the observable instead of the state for quick calculations.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{35}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Measuring $Y$}
Which unitary $U$ satisfies $UYU^\dagger = Z$, so that measuring $Z$ after applying $U$ measures $Y$?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$U = S$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$U = HS^\dagger$ (first $S^\dagger$, then $H$) \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$U = SH$ (first $H$, then $S$) & \optlabel{D}\,$U = H$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $U = HS^\dagger$ (first $S^\dagger$, then $H$)

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Clifford conjugation of Paulis by $S$ and $H$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $SXS^\dagger = Y$, $HXH = Z$, $HYH = -Y$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} With $S = \operatorname{diag}(1, i)$: $SXS^\dagger = \begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{psmallmatrix}\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\0&-i\end{psmallmatrix} = \begin{psmallmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{psmallmatrix} = Y$,
hence $S^\dagger YS = X$. Therefore
\[ (HS^\dagger)\,Y\,(HS^\dagger)^\dagger = H\,(S^\dagger YS)\,H = HXH = Z . \]
In circuit order: apply $S^\dagger$, then $H$, then measure in the computational basis. $H$ alone maps $Y \to -Y$; $S$ maps $Y \to SYS^\dagger = -X$;
neither diagonalises $Y$. (Verified numerically in \texttt{verify\_answers.py}.)

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $SYS^\dagger = -X$, not $Z$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $SH$ in that order maps $Y$ elsewhere ($SHYHS^\dagger = -SYS^\dagger = X$).
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $HYH = -Y$: still not diagonal.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Measure $Y$: apply $S^\dagger$, then $H$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 36 and 37}
A two-qubit transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian $H = -Z_0Z_1 - \tfrac12(X_0 + X_1)$ (the notebook's \texttt{"tfim"} model with $N = 2$,
$J = 1$, $h = 0.5$) is treated with a tiny hardware-efficient circuit: starting from $\ket{00}$, apply $R_Y(\theta_0)$ to qubit 0 and $R_Y(\theta_1)$
to qubit 1, then a CNOT with control 0 and target 1. The angles are $\theta_0 = \pi/2$, $\theta_1 = 0$.
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{36}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Two-qubit Ising: trial energy}
The energy $\braket{\psi|H|\psi}$ of the prepared state is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$-1$ & \optlabel{B}\,$0$ & \optlabel{C}\,$-\sqrt2 \approx -1.414$ & \optlabel{D}\,$-1.5$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $-1$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Term-by-term energy of a Bell state.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E = -\braket{Z_0Z_1} - \tfrac12(\braket{X_0} + \braket{X_1})$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The circuit prepares the Bell state $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} + \ket{11})$ (Q.27). Term by term: $\braket{Z_0Z_1} = 1$ (both components have equal bits);
$\braket{X_0} = 0$ because $X_0$ maps $\ket{00} \to \ket{10}$ and $\ket{11} \to \ket{01}$, states orthogonal to the Bell state; likewise $\braket{X_1} = 0$.
$E = -1\cdot1 - \tfrac12(0 + 0) = -1$. The state wins the full $ZZ$ energy but none of the field energy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $\braket{Z_0Z_1} = 1$ contributes $-1$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $-\sqrt2$ is the exact ground energy, not reached by this state.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $-1.5$ assumes $\braket{X_0} = 1$ or similar; both are 0 for $\ket{\Phi^+}$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Entanglement alone is not enough: the ansatz must also capture the field terms.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{37}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Two-qubit Ising: exact $E_0$}
The exact ground-state energy $E_0$ of this $H$, and the relative error of the prepared state, are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$-1$; $0\,\%$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$-\sqrt2 \approx -1.414$; $29.3\,\%$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$-\sqrt2$; $41.4\,\%$ & \optlabel{D}\,$-1.5$; $33.3\,\%$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $-\sqrt2 \approx -1.414$; $29.3\,\%$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Symmetry blocks; $2\times2$ diagonalisation; relative error.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\lambda = \pm\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ for $\begin{psmallmatrix}-a&-b\\-b&a\end{psmallmatrix}$; rel.\ error $= (E - E_0)/|E_0|$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $H$ commutes with $X_0X_1$, so it splits into two $2\times2$ blocks. The ground state lies in the block $X_0X_1 = +1$, spanned by
$\ket{\Phi^+} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00} + \ket{11})$ and $\ket{\Psi^+} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{01} + \ket{10})$. Matrix elements: $\braket{\Phi^+|H|\Phi^+} = -1$ (from $-Z_0Z_1$),
$\braket{\Psi^+|H|\Psi^+} = +1$, and since $X_0\ket{\Psi^+} = X_1\ket{\Psi^+} = \ket{\Phi^+}$: $\braket{\Phi^+|H|\Psi^+} = -\tfrac12(1 + 1) = -1$. Eigenvalues of $\begin{psmallmatrix}-1&-1\\-1&1\end{psmallmatrix}$: $\pm\sqrt2$, so $E_0 = -\sqrt2$
(free-fermion formula and exact diagonalisation agree). Relative error $\frac{-1 - (-\sqrt2)}{\sqrt2} = \frac{0.414}{1.414} = 29.3\,\%$.
Choosing $\theta_1 \neq 0$ (or more layers) lets the ansatz mix in $\ket{\Psi^+}$ and lower the energy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $-1$ is the trial energy, not $E_0$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $41.4\,\%$ divides by $|E|$ instead of $|E_0|$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $-1.5$ ignores the off-diagonal coupling.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Use symmetries to shrink an eigenproblem before solving it.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{38}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Pauli basis size}
Every Hermitian $2^n\times2^n$ matrix is a real linear combination of the $n$-qubit Pauli strings. For $n = 4$ the number of Pauli strings,
and the number actually needed for the notebook's H$_2$ Hamiltonian, are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$256$ and $256$ & \optlabel{B}\,$64$ and $15$ & \optlabel{C}\,$16$ and $15$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$256$ and $15$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $256$ and $15$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Pauli basis of operator space; sparsity of molecular Hamiltonians.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\#\text{Pauli strings} = 4^n$; $c_P = 2^{-n}\operatorname{tr}(PH)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Each qubit carries one of $I, X, Y, Z$: $4^n$ strings; $n = 4$: $256$. They form an orthogonal basis of the $4^n$-dimensional space of
$2^n\times2^n$ matrices ($\operatorname{tr}(PQ) = 2^n\delta_{PQ}$), so $c_P = 2^{-n}\operatorname{tr}(PH)$. Molecular Hamiltonians are \emph{sparse} in this basis:
H$_2$ needs only 15 of the 256 (symmetries such as particle-number and spin conservation remove the rest).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] H$_2$ uses only 15 strings.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $64 = 4^3$ would be the number of Pauli strings on 3 qubits, not 4.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $16 = 2^4$ is the state dimension.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $4^n$ possible terms, but physical Hamiltonians use few.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{39}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{Simultaneous measurement}
\textbf{Statement I:} Two Pauli strings either commute or anticommute.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} A set of mutually commuting Pauli strings can be measured simultaneously after one common basis change.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\optlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} Both Statement I and Statement II are true

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Pauli commutation; simultaneous measurement.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $PQ = \pm QP$; commuting observables share eigenbases.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is true:} position by position the factors commute or anticommute, so $PQ = (-1)^kQP$ with $k$ = number of anticommuting positions.
\textbf{II is true:} commuting Hermitian operators share an eigenbasis; a Clifford circuit rotating that basis to the computational basis lets
one set of shots estimate all of them (for qubit-wise commuting sets this circuit is just single-qubit rotations). This is the basis of
measurement grouping. Answer: (A).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] needs both statements false; both are true.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] needs I true and II false; II is true.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] needs I false and II true; I is true.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Grouping commuting terms saves shots.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{40}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Energy variance}
For $H = -Z + \tfrac12X$ (one qubit), the energy variance $\mathrm{Var}(H) = \braket{H^2} - \braket H^2$ in the state $\ket0$, and in the exact ground state, are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.25$ and $1.25$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1.25$ and $0$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.25$ and $0$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0$ and $0.25$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.25$ and $0$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Energy variance; zero-variance principle.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathrm{Var}(H) = \braket{H^2} - \braket H^2$; $(aZ + bX)^2 = (a^2 + b^2)I$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $H^2 = Z^2 - \tfrac12(ZX + XZ) + \tfrac14X^2 = \tfrac54I$ (the cross terms cancel because $ZX = -XZ$). So $\braket{H^2} = 1.25$ in every state.
For $\ket0$: $\braket H = -1$, variance $1.25 - 1 = 0.25$. For the ground state: $\braket H = -\sqrt{5/4}$, $\braket H^2 = 1.25$, variance $0$.
\emph{Zero-variance principle}: exact eigenstates have zero energy variance, so the variance measures how far a VQE state is from an
eigenstate --- and how many shots an energy estimate needs (shot noise $\propto \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}/S}$).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] The exact eigenstate has zero variance.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1.25$ is $\braket{H^2}$, not the variance.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Swaps the two states.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Variance $\to 0$ signals an eigenstate and fewer shots needed.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\newpage

\begin{sectionbanner}SECTION C \enspace$\cdot$\enspace VQE Fundamentals \hfill Q.41--60\end{sectionbanner}

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{41}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Energy below $E_0$ = bug}
A VQE run with \emph{exact} expectation values (no shots, no noise) reports $E(\boldsymbol\theta) = -15.10$ for the 15-qubit Ising chain whose exact ground
energy is $E_0 = -15.0825$. The most likely explanation is
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] the optimizer found a state better than the exact ground state
\item[\optlabel{B}] a deeper ansatz always produces energies below the exact value
\item[\correctlabel{C}] an error in the Hamiltonian, the reference energy or the state normalisation --- a correct calculation cannot go below $E_0$
\item[\optlabel{D}] shot noise pushed the estimate below $E_0$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} an error in the Hamiltonian, the reference energy or the state normalisation --- a correct calculation cannot go below $E_0$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Variational bound as a correctness check.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E(\boldsymbol\theta) = \braket{\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)|H|\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)} \ge E_0$ for normalised states.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Variational principle: for every normalised state $\braket{\psi|H|\psi} \ge E_0$ (Q.7). Exact expectation values of a normalised circuit state
(unitary gates, Q.28) therefore can never fall below $E_0$. A value below it signals a bug: a wrong Hamiltonian term or sign, a wrong
reference, or an expectation value of an unnormalised vector. With shots, single estimates \emph{can} fluctuate below $E_0$, but the
question excludes shots. This is why the notebook prints ``the VQE energy must stay $\ge E_0$''.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] No normalised state lies below $E_0$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] More layers approach $E_0$ from above, never cross it.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Shot noise is excluded (exact expectation values).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} An energy below the exact reference is a bug detector.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{42}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Rayleigh--Ritz bounds}
In the Rayleigh--Ritz method, $H$ is diagonalised inside an $m$-dimensional trial subspace, giving Ritz values $\varepsilon_1 \le \dots \le \varepsilon_m$. Which
statement is correct?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Only $\varepsilon_1$ is bounded; the other Ritz values can lie below the exact eigenvalues
\item[\optlabel{B}] The Ritz values are lower bounds to the exact eigenvalues
\item[\correctlabel{C}] $\varepsilon_k \ge E_{k-1}$ for every $k$: each Ritz value is an upper bound to the corresponding exact eigenvalue
\item[\optlabel{D}] The Ritz values are exact whenever $m \ge 2$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $\varepsilon_k \ge E_{k-1}$ for every $k$: each Ritz value is an upper bound to the corresponding exact eigenvalue

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Rayleigh--Ritz / Hylleraas--Undheim--MacDonald theorem.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\varepsilon_k \ge E_{k-1}$ (min--max theorem).

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Write $P$ for the projector onto the trial space. By the Courant--Fischer min--max theorem the $k$-th eigenvalue of $PHP$ restricted to the
subspace is $\ge$ the $k$-th eigenvalue of $H$ (Hylleraas--Undheim--MacDonald theorem): $\varepsilon_k \ge E_{k-1}$ (labelling exact levels
$E_0 \le E_1 \le \dots$). For $k = 1$ this is the variational principle. Enlarging the subspace can only lower every Ritz value. The passage for
Q.59 and Q.60 is a Rayleigh--Ritz calculation with $m = 2$; there $\varepsilon_1$ happens to be exact because the ground state lies in the subspace.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] All Ritz values are upper bounds, not only the first.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Upper, not lower, bounds.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Exact only if the subspace contains the eigenvectors.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Restricting the state space can only raise energies.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{43}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Hardware-efficient ansatz counts}
The notebook's hardware-efficient ansatz uses $L$ layers of [$R_Y$ on every qubit, CNOT ladder over neighbours] plus a final $R_Y$ layer. For
$N = 10$ qubits and $L = 3$, the numbers of parameters, CNOTs and gates are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$40$, $30$ and $70$ & \optlabel{B}\,$30$, $27$ and $57$ & \optlabel{C}\,$40$, $9$ and $49$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$40$, $27$ and $67$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $40$, $27$ and $67$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Hardware-efficient ansatz counts.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} parameters $(L+1)N$; CNOTs $L(N-1)$; gates sum of both.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Parameters: one angle per $R_Y$: $(L + 1)N = 4\cdot10 = 40$. CNOTs: each ladder has $N - 1 = 9$ CNOTs, $L$ ladders: $27$.
Gates: $40 + 27 = 67$ (the notebook's estimate \texttt{num\_parameters + ANSATZ\_LAYERS * (n\_qubits - 1)}).
Default ($N = 15$, $L = 2$): $45$ parameters, $28$ CNOTs, $73$ gates --- exactly the recorded statistics \texttt{ry 45, cx 28}.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Uses $N$ CNOTs per ladder (a closed ring); the notebook's ladder is open.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Forgets the final rotation layer ($LN = 30$).
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $9$ CNOTs is a single ladder; with $L = 3$ layers there are three ladders, $27$ CNOTs.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Default: 45 parameters, 28 CNOTs, 73 gates.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{44}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Hartree--Fock preparation}
The UCC kernel starts with \texttt{x(qubits[0]); x(qubits[1])}. In the Jordan--Wigner picture with spin-orbitals ordered (orbital 0 $\alpha$, orbital 0 $\beta$,
orbital 1 $\alpha$, orbital 1 $\beta$), this prepares
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] the state with both electrons in the antibonding orbital
\item[\optlabel{B}] an equal superposition of all 2-electron determinants
\item[\correctlabel{C}] the Hartree--Fock determinant $\ket{1100}$: both electrons in the lower (bonding) spatial orbital, one with each spin
\item[\optlabel{D}] a triplet state with both electrons spin-up
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} the Hartree--Fock determinant $\ket{1100}$: both electrons in the lower (bonding) spatial orbital, one with each spin

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Jordan--Wigner occupation; Hartree--Fock reference.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\ket{n_0n_1n_2n_3}$, $n_j = 1$ occupied; HF: lowest $N_e$ spin-orbitals filled.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Under Jordan--Wigner, qubit $j$ in $\ket1$ means spin-orbital $j$ is occupied. $X$ on qubits 0 and 1 turns $\ket{0000}$ into $\ket{1100}$: spin-orbitals
0 ($\sigma_g\alpha$) and 1 ($\sigma_g\beta$) occupied. This closed-shell determinant is the restricted Hartree--Fock state; its energy
$\braket{1100|H|1100} = -1.116759$ Ha is the HF energy (Q.48). VQE starts there ($\theta = 0$) and the double excitation adds the correlation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Antibonding occupation is $\ket{0011}$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Two $X$ gates create one basis state, not a superposition.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Spin-orbitals 0 and 1 are $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of the same orbital: a singlet-type closed shell.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Initial state matters: HF is the natural VQE starting point for molecules.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{45}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Two-state energy formula}
Let $\ket u$, $\ket v$ be orthonormal, $H_{uu} = a$, $H_{vv} = c$, $H_{uv} = H_{vu} = b$ (real). For the trial state $\ket{\psi(\theta)} = \cos\theta\ket u - \sin\theta\ket v$, the energy is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$a\cos^2\theta + c\sin^2\theta - b\sin2\theta$ & \optlabel{B}\,$a\cos^2\theta - c\sin^2\theta$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$a\cos\theta + c\sin\theta - b$ & \optlabel{D}\,$a\cos^2\theta + c\sin^2\theta + b\sin2\theta$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $a\cos^2\theta + c\sin^2\theta - b\sin2\theta$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Energy of a two-state superposition.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E = a\cos^2\theta + c\sin^2\theta - b\sin2\theta$; $\tan2\theta^* = \frac{2b}{c - a}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $E = \braket{\psi|H|\psi} = \cos^2\theta\,H_{uu} + \sin^2\theta\,H_{vv} - \sin\theta\cos\theta(H_{uv} + H_{vu}) = a\cos^2\theta + c\sin^2\theta - 2b\sin\theta\cos\theta$,
and $2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin2\theta$. The minus sign comes from the $-\sin\theta$ amplitude. Minimising: $E'(\theta) = (c - a)\sin2\theta - 2b\cos2\theta = 0$,
i.e.\ $\tan2\theta^* = \frac{2b}{c - a}$, and the minimum equals the lower eigenvalue of $\begin{psmallmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{psmallmatrix}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Drops the cross term and has a wrong sign.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Amplitudes, not probabilities: energies need squares.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $+b\sin2\theta$ is for the state $\cos\theta\ket u + \sin\theta\ket v$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Two-level problems reduce VQE to one angle.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{46}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{VQE $\leftrightarrow$ code}
Match each VQE ingredient (List-I) with the code in \texttt{VQE.ipynb} that implements it (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & Hartree--Fock reference state & \textbf{(1)} & \texttt{minimize(energy, initial\_theta, method="COBYLA", ...)} \\
\textbf{(Q)} & energy $E(\boldsymbol\theta) = \braket{\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)|H|\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)}$ & \textbf{(2)} & \texttt{coefficient * cudaq.SpinOperator.from\_word(word)}, summed \\
\textbf{(R)} & classical parameter update & \textbf{(3)} & \texttt{x(qubits[0]); x(qubits[1])} \\
\textbf{(S)} & Hamiltonian as a sum of Pauli strings & \textbf{(4)} & \texttt{cudaq.observe(kernel, hamiltonian, *args).expectation()} \\

\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$2
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Mapping VQE to the notebook's code.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E(\boldsymbol\theta) \leftarrow$ \texttt{observe}; $\boldsymbol\theta \leftarrow$ \texttt{minimize}; $H \leftarrow$ \texttt{SpinOperator.from\_word}.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item P: two $X$ gates occupy spin-orbitals 0 and 1 (3).
\item Q: \texttt{cudaq.observe} evaluates $\sum_kc_k\braket{P_k}$ for the ansatz kernel; \texttt{.expectation()} returns the number (4).
\item R: SciPy's \texttt{minimize} proposes new angles from the returned energies (1).
\item S: \texttt{build\_spin\_operator} turns each \texttt{(coefficient, word)} pair into a \texttt{SpinOperator} and adds them (2).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] R$\to$2, S$\to$1 calls the Hamiltonian builder the optimizer.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] P$\to$4: the HF state is prepared by gates, not computed by \texttt{observe}.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Q$\to$1, R$\to$4 swaps the quantum and the classical step.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Quantum: prepare and measure; classical: update angles.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{47}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Energy from Pauli averages}
$H = 0.5\,Z_0 - 0.3\,Z_1 + 0.2\,X_0X_1$. A trial state has $\braket{Z_0} = 0.6$, $\braket{Z_1} = -0.2$ and $\braket{X_0X_1} = 0.5$. Its energy is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.34$ & \optlabel{B}\,$1.3$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$0.46$ & \optlabel{D}\,$0.26$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $0.46$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Linearity of expectation values.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E = \sum_kc_k\braket{P_k}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Linearity: $E = 0.5(0.6) - 0.3(-0.2) + 0.2(0.5) = 0.30 + 0.06 + 0.10 = 0.46$. Each $\braket{P_k}$ is estimated separately (or in commuting groups) and the
energy is the coefficient-weighted sum --- exactly what \texttt{cudaq.observe} does term by term.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.34$ uses $-0.3\times0.2$ (sign error).
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1.3$ sums $|c_k|$ only.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.26$ drops the $XX$ term.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Multiply each measured Pauli average by its coefficient and add.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{48}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{HF energy from $Z$ terms}
Only the identity and the $Z$-type terms of the notebook's H$_2$ Hamiltonian contribute to $\braket{1100|H|1100}$. With coefficients
$c_{IIII} = -0.097066$, $c_{ZIII} = c_{IZII} = 0.171413$, $c_{IIZI} = c_{IIIZ} = -0.223432$, $c_{ZZII} = 0.168689$, $c_{ZIZI} = c_{IZIZ} = 0.120625$,
$c_{ZIIZ} = c_{IZZI} = 0.165928$, $c_{IIZZ} = 0.174413$, the Hartree--Fock energy is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$-1.137284$ Ha & \optlabel{B}\,$-0.097066$ Ha & \optlabel{C}\,$+0.462618$ Ha & \correctlabel{D}\,$-1.116759$ Ha
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $-1.116759$ Ha

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Diagonal elements from $Z$-type terms.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $Z_j\ket{n} = (1 - 2n_j)\ket n$; off-diagonal strings give 0 on the diagonal.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} On $\ket{1100}$: $Z_0 = Z_1 = -1$ (occupied), $Z_2 = Z_3 = +1$. The $XY$-type terms flip bits and have zero diagonal element.
\[ E_{\mathrm{HF}} = -0.097066 - 2(0.171413) - 2(0.223432) + 0.168689 - 2(0.120625) - 2(0.165928) + 0.174413 . \]
$= -0.097066 - 0.342826 - 0.446863 + 0.168689 - 0.241250 - 0.331856 + 0.174413 = -1.116759$ Ha.
(Signs: $Z_0Z_1 = (+1)$, $Z_2Z_3 = (+1)$, mixed pairs $(-1)$.) $-1.137284$ is FCI; $+0.462618$ is $\braket{0011|H|0011}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $-1.137284$ is FCI, below HF.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Only the identity term.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $+0.462618$ is $\braket{0011|H|0011}$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} HF energy = expectation of $H$ in one determinant.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{49}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{Exactness of the UCC ansatz}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} The notebook's one-parameter UCC ansatz can reach the exact (FCI) ground energy of its H$_2$ Hamiltonian.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} The exact ground state of that Hamiltonian lies in $\mathrm{span}\{\ket{1100}, \ket{0011}\}$, and $\cos\theta\ket{1100} - \sin\theta\ket{0011}$ covers every
real normalised vector of that span (up to sign).
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\correctlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Expressiveness of an ansatz; exact subspace.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\ket{\psi_0} = 0.9937\ket{1100} - 0.1125\ket{0011}$; $\theta^* = 0.112783$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{R is true:} exact diagonalisation of the $16\times16$ matrix gives a ground state with weights $0.98733$ on $\ket{1100}$ and $0.01267$ on $\ket{0011}$
and nothing else (particle-number, spin and spatial symmetry forbid single excitations and the other determinants). Any real unit vector
$(\cos\theta, -\sin\theta)$ in that plane is reached by some $\theta$.
\textbf{A follows:} at $\theta^* = 0.112783$ the energy equals $-1.137283834$ Ha to $10^{-15}$ (NumPy and CUDA-Q). R explains A. Answer: (A).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] needs A and R both true but R not explaining A; R is exactly why A holds.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] needs A true and R false; R is true.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] needs A false and R true; A is true.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} An ansatz is exact if it spans the subspace containing the ground state.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{50}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Energy of $\ket{0\dots0}$}
For the default Ising chain ($N = 15$, $J = 1$, $h = 0.5$, $H = -J\sum Z_iZ_{i+1} - h\sum X_i$), the energy of $\ket{00\dots0}$ --- close to where the
hardware-efficient ansatz starts, since its initial angles are drawn from $\mathcal N(0, 0.1^2)$ --- is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$-15$ & \optlabel{B}\,$-21.5$ & \optlabel{C}\,$-7.5$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$-14$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $-14$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Energy of a product state for the Ising chain.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\braket{0\dots0|Z_iZ_{i+1}|0\dots0} = 1$, $\braket{X_i} = 0$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} On $\ket{0\dots0}$ every $Z_iZ_{i+1} = +1$: $14$ bonds give $-14$. $\braket{X_i} = 0$ for a computational basis state. So $E = -14$, compared with
$E_0 = -15.0825$: the field term contributes about $-1.08$ in the true ground state through small admixtures of flipped spins.
Small random angles start the optimizer close to this classical ordered state (not exactly at it, to break symmetries).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $-15$ counts 15 bonds; an open chain has 14.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $-21.5$ adds $-h$ per site, but $\braket{X_i} = 0$ on a basis state.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $-7.5$ uses only the field.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The ordered product state already captures most of the energy.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{51}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Gradient cost}
Each of the 45 angles of the default hardware-efficient ansatz enters exactly one $R_Y$ gate. The number of circuit evaluations for one exact
parameter-shift gradient, and for one forward finite-difference gradient (L-BFGS-B), are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$90$ and $90$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$90$ and $46$ & \optlabel{C}\,$2$ and $46$ & \optlabel{D}\,$45$ and $46$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $90$ and $46$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Gradient cost: parameter shift versus finite differences.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} shift: $2n_p$ runs (one gate per parameter); forward differences: $n_p + 1$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Parameter shift for a gate $e^{-i\theta Y/2}$: $\partial_\theta E = \tfrac12[E(\theta + \tfrac\pi2) - E(\theta - \tfrac\pi2)]$ --- 2 evaluations per parameter, exact: $2\times45 = 90$.
Forward differences: $E(\boldsymbol\theta)$ once plus one shifted evaluation per parameter: $45 + 1 = 46$ (the notebook's table: ``N\_params + 1
runs per gradient''), approximate and fragile under shot noise. COBYLA (default) uses no gradients at all.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Finite differences need one extra run per parameter plus the base point.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Two runs suffice only for one parameter.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Parameter shift needs two runs per parameter.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Gradients cost $O(n_p)$ circuit runs.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{52}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{COBYLA; best-of-history}
\textbf{Statement I:} COBYLA needs no gradient evaluations.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} The notebook reports the energy of the optimizer's final point \texttt{opt.x} as the VQE energy.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\correctlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\optlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} Statement I is true, but Statement II is false

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Optimizer properties; best-of-history bookkeeping.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} \texttt{best\_index = argmin(energy\_history)}.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is true:} COBYLA builds linear models from function values inside a trust region (initial radius \texttt{rhobeg = 0.3} in the notebook).
\textbf{II is false:} the code stores every evaluation and uses \texttt{best\_index = int(np.argmin(energy\_history))}; the reported energy and the sampled
state belong to the best evaluated angles, which need not be \texttt{opt.x}. Answer: (C).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] needs both statements true; II is false.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] needs both statements false; I is true.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] needs I false and II true; I true, II false.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Report the best evaluated point, not the optimizer's last guess.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{53}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Chemical accuracy check}
Four VQE runs on the notebook's H$_2$ Hamiltonian (exact expectation values; FCI $= -1.137284$ Ha) report the energies below. Which one is a valid,
chemically accurate result?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$-1.11676$ Ha & \correctlabel{B}\,$-1.13600$ Ha & \optlabel{C}\,$-1.13500$ Ha & \optlabel{D}\,$-1.13900$ Ha
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $-1.13600$ Ha

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Validity and chemical accuracy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $0 \le E - E_{\mathrm{FCI}} < 1.6$ mHa.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Errors $E - E_{\mathrm{FCI}}$: $-1.13600$: $+1.28$ mHa (above FCI, below $1.6$ mHa: chemically accurate, valid).
$-1.13500$: $+2.28$ mHa (valid but not chemically accurate). $-1.11676$: $+20.5$ mHa, the Hartree--Fock energy ($\theta = 0$).
$-1.13900$: $-1.72$ mHa, \emph{below} FCI, impossible with exact expectation values (Q.41).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] That is the HF energy: $20.5$ mHa error.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $2.28$ mHa error: above threshold.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Below FCI: violates the variational principle.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Valid means $\ge E_0$; accurate means within 1.6 mHa.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{54}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Measurement grouping}
The notebook's H$_2$ Hamiltonian has the identity, 10 $Z$-type terms and 4 terms $\texttt{XXYY}$, $\texttt{XYYX}$, $\texttt{YXXY}$, $\texttt{YYXX}$. With
\emph{qubit-wise commuting} grouping, the minimum number of measurement settings is ..., and with general commuting grouping ...
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$5$; $2$ & \optlabel{B}\,$15$; $5$ & \optlabel{C}\,$2$; $1$ & \optlabel{D}\,$4$; $1$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $5$; $2$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Measurement grouping.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} settings = number of groups (identity needs none).

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The identity needs no measurement. All $Z$-type terms are qubit-wise commuting: one setting (plain $Z$ measurement). No two of the four
exchange terms are qubit-wise commuting (Q.29), so each needs its own setting: $1 + 4 = 5$. Under general commutation the four exchange
terms commute pairwise and form one group (measured with an entangling basis change), so $1 + 1 = 2$. (Whether the $Z$-group and the
exchange group could merge: $\texttt{ZIII}$ anticommutes with $\texttt{XXYY}$, so no.) Grouping directly reduces the shot cost of VQE.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $15$ measures every term separately including the identity.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $2$ is the general-commuting count; QWC needs 5.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Ignores the $Z$ group or merges incompatible groups.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Better grouping $\Rightarrow$ fewer settings $\Rightarrow$ fewer shots.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{55}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Recorded relative error}
In the previously recorded default run, $E_{\mathrm{VQE}} = -15.0533898284$ and the exact $E_0 = -15.0825179883$. The relative error is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$1.93\,\%$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$0.193\,\%$ & \optlabel{C}\,$0.0291\,\%$ & \optlabel{D}\,$-0.193\,\%$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $0.193\,\%$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Absolute and relative error.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} rel.\ error $= (E_{\mathrm{VQE}} - E_0)/|E_0|$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Absolute error $E_{\mathrm{VQE}} - E_0 = -15.0533898 + 15.0825180 = 0.0291282$ (positive, as the variational principle requires). Relative:
$0.0291282/15.0825180 = 0.00193 = 0.193\,\%$ --- the notebook prints ``2.913e-02 (relative 0.193\%)''. Note that TFIM energies are dimensionless
(in units of $J$); chemical accuracy does not apply to this model.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $1.93\,\%$ is ten times too large: $0.0291/15.08 = 0.00193 = 0.193\,\%$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.0291$ is the absolute error read as a percentage.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Negative would mean below $E_0$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Relative errors can hide what matters; compare with a baseline (Q.79).
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{56}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Real ansatz for real $H$}
The notebook's hardware-efficient ansatz uses only $R_Y$ rotations and CNOTs, so it produces states with \emph{real} amplitudes. Why is this
adequate for its Ising and H$_2$ Hamiltonians?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Complex amplitudes cannot be measured, so they are never needed
\item[\correctlabel{B}] Both Hamiltonians are real symmetric matrices, so a ground state can always be chosen real
\item[\optlabel{C}] Real amplitudes always give lower energies than complex ones
\item[\optlabel{D}] CNOT gates generate all complex phases automatically
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} Both Hamiltonians are real symmetric matrices, so a ground state can always be chosen real

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Real Hamiltonians and real ansätze.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $H = H^{\mathsf T}$ real $\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{Re}\,v$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,v$ are eigenvectors.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $R_Y(\theta)$ and CNOT have real matrices, so they map real vectors to real vectors. The Ising Hamiltonian ($Z$ and $X$ only) is real; the H$_2$
Hamiltonian is real too ($\texttt{XXYY}$-type strings contain an even number of $Y$'s, each $Y$ contributes $\pm i$, so the products are real).
For a real symmetric $H$ the real and imaginary parts of an eigenvector are eigenvectors themselves, so a real ground state exists. For
Hamiltonians with genuinely complex matrix elements (e.g.\ magnetic fields) a real ansatz would fail.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Complex phases do affect energies through interference.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Real and complex ansätze give the same minimum for real $H$; neither is always lower.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] CNOT is a real permutation matrix.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Match the ansatz's number field to the Hamiltonian's.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{57}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Symmetry breaking}
The recorded optimised state of the Ising chain gives $\ket{000\dots0}$ with probability $0.70$ but $\ket{111\dots1}$ (not in the top 8) with nearly zero
probability, although $H$ is symmetric under flipping all spins. The best explanation is
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] $\ket{111\dots1}$ has a higher energy than $\ket{000\dots0}$
\item[\optlabel{B}] the exact ground state contains only $\ket{000\dots0}$
\item[\optlabel{C}] the simulator has a bias towards $\ket0$
\item[\correctlabel{D}] for $h < J$ the two ordered configurations are nearly degenerate; VQE settled on one of them (symmetry breaking), which costs only an energy exponentially small in $N$
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} for $h < J$ the two ordered configurations are nearly degenerate; VQE settled on one of them (symmetry breaking), which costs only an energy exponentially small in $N$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Spontaneous symmetry breaking in finite VQE.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $[H, \prod_iX_i] = 0$; splitting $\propto (h/J)^N$ for $h < J$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\prod_iX_i$ commutes with $H$, so the exact ground state is symmetric: $P(0\dots0) = P(1\dots1)$. For $h < J$ it is close to the ``cat'' state
$\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{\Uparrow} + \ket{\Downarrow})$ (dressed by spin flips), whose symmetric and antisymmetric combinations are split only by an energy that
decreases exponentially with $N$. A shallow ansatz started near $\ket{0\dots0}$ cannot build the cat state cheaply and settles near one branch, as the
notebook's text explains; the energy cost is tiny compared with the recorded error $0.029$. Both configurations have the same energy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Both configurations have energy $-14$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] The exact ground state is symmetric between the two configurations.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] No such bias: the state is set by the optimised angles.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} A broken-symmetry VQE state can still have an excellent energy.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{58}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Optimizers}
Match each optimizer offered by the notebook (List-I) with its working principle (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & COBYLA & \textbf{(1)} & successive line searches along a set of conjugate directions, derivative-free \\
\textbf{(Q)} & Nelder--Mead & \textbf{(2)} & quasi-Newton method with a limited-memory Hessian estimate, using gradients (finite differences here) and box bounds \\
\textbf{(R)} & Powell & \textbf{(3)} & linear models of the objective inside a shrinking trust region, derivative-free \\
\textbf{(S)} & L-BFGS-B & \textbf{(4)} & a simplex of $n+1$ points updated by reflection, expansion and contraction \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \optlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$2 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Classical optimizers.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} COBYLA: trust region; NM: simplex; Powell: line searches; L-BFGS-B: quasi-Newton.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item P: COBYLA = Constrained Optimization BY Linear Approximation, trust region (3) --- default, \texttt{maxiter = 300}, \texttt{rhobeg = 0.3}.
\item Q: Nelder--Mead simplex (4) --- \texttt{maxfev} budget.
\item R: Powell's conjugate-direction method (1).
\item S: L-BFGS-B (2) --- the only one needing gradients; without analytic gradients SciPy uses $n + 1$ evaluations per gradient.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Q$\to$1, R$\to$4 swaps Nelder--Mead and Powell.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] P$\to$4, Q$\to$3 swaps COBYLA and Nelder--Mead.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] R$\to$2, S$\to$1 calls Powell gradient-based.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Derivative-free methods dominate VQE with noisy energies.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 59 and 60}
In the notebook's H$_2$ example the UCC state $\ket{\psi(\theta)} = \cos\theta\ket{1100} - \sin\theta\ket{0011}$ only involves two basis states. Within
this two-dimensional space the Hamiltonian is the real $2\times2$ matrix
\[ \begin{pmatrix} H_{11} & H_{12}\\ H_{12} & H_{22}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1.116759 & 0.181210\\ 0.181210 & 0.462618\end{pmatrix}\ \text{Ha}, \]
with $H_{11} = \braket{1100|H|1100}$, $H_{22} = \braket{0011|H|0011}$, $H_{12} = \braket{1100|H|0011}$ (computed from the notebook's 15 Pauli terms), so that
$E(\theta) = H_{11}\cos^2\theta + H_{22}\sin^2\theta - H_{12}\sin2\theta$.
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{59}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{H$_2$ two-level reduction: $E_0$}
The lowest eigenvalue of the $2\times2$ matrix --- the best energy the UCC ansatz can reach --- is
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$-1.116759$ Ha & \optlabel{B}\,$+0.483143$ Ha & \optlabel{C}\,$-0.654141$ Ha & \correctlabel{D}\,$-1.137284$ Ha
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $-1.137284$ Ha

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Eigenvalues of a $2\times2$ symmetric matrix.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\lambda_\pm = \frac{a+c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{c-a}{2}\right)^2 + b^2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} For $\begin{psmallmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{psmallmatrix}$: $\lambda_\pm = \frac{a+c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{c-a}{2}\right)^2 + b^2}$.
$\frac{a+c}{2} = \frac{-1.116759 + 0.462618}{2} = -0.327071$; $\frac{c-a}{2} = 0.789689$; $\sqrt{0.789689^2 + 0.181210^2} = \sqrt{0.623608 + 0.032837} = 0.810213$.
$\lambda_- = -0.327071 - 0.810213 = -1.137284$ Ha $= E_{\mathrm{FCI}}$; $\lambda_+ = +0.483143$ (an excited state of the full Hamiltonian, too).
The coupling $H_{12}$ lowers the energy below $H_{11} = E_{\mathrm{HF}}$ by $20.5$ mHa, the correlation energy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] That is $H_{11} = E_{\mathrm{HF}}$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] The upper eigenvalue.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $-0.654141 = H_{11} + H_{22}$ is the trace (sum of both eigenvalues), not the lower eigenvalue.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Two-level reduction reproduces FCI exactly for H$_2$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{60}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{H$_2$: optimal angle, weights}
The optimal angle $\theta^*$ and the probability of measuring $\ket{0011}$ in the optimal state are
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\theta^* \approx 0.2295$ rad and $0.0518$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$\theta^* \approx 0.1128$ rad and $0.0127$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$\theta^* \approx -0.1128$ rad and $0.0127$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\theta^* \approx 0.1128$ rad and $0.1125$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $\theta^* \approx 0.1128$ rad and $0.0127$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Optimal mixing angle and weights.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\tan2\theta^* = \frac{2H_{12}}{H_{22} - H_{11}}$; $P(\ket{0011}) = \sin^2\theta^*$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $E'(\theta) = (H_{22} - H_{11})\sin2\theta - 2H_{12}\cos2\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \tan2\theta^* = \frac{2H_{12}}{H_{22} - H_{11}} = \frac{0.362420}{1.579377} = 0.229471$,
$2\theta^* = 0.225566$, $\theta^* = 0.112783$ rad (the minimum, $E'' > 0$). Probability of $\ket{0011}$: $\sin^2\theta^* = 0.0127$ (amplitude $-0.1125$).
So the exact H$_2$ ground state is $98.7\,\%$ Hartree--Fock and $1.3\,\%$ doubly excited; this small admixture is worth $20.5$ mHa.
Negative $\theta$ would raise the energy; $0.2295$ is $\tan2\theta^*$, not $\theta^*$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Confuses $\tan2\theta^*$ with $\theta^*$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Negative $\theta$ raises the energy.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $0.1125$ is the amplitude's modulus, not the probability.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} $1.3\,\%$ admixture $\to$ $20.5$ mHa correlation energy.
\end{solbox}
\qsep
