\begin{sectionbanner}SECTION D \enspace$\cdot$\enspace Advanced VQE and Implementation \hfill Q.61--80\end{sectionbanner}

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{61}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Jordan--Wigner $a_j^\dagger$}
With the Jordan--Wigner transformation $a_j^\dagger = \big(\prod_{k<j}Z_k\big)\,\tfrac12(X_j - iY_j)$ (qubit $\ket1$ = occupied), the creation operator $a_2^\dagger$ on
4 spin-orbitals becomes
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\tfrac12\,Z_0Z_1(X_2 + iY_2)$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\tfrac12(X_2 - iY_2)$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$\tfrac12\,Z_3(X_2 - iY_2)$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$\tfrac12\,Z_0Z_1(X_2 - iY_2)$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $\tfrac12\,Z_0Z_1(X_2 - iY_2)$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Jordan--Wigner transformation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $a_j^\dagger = Z_0\cdots Z_{j-1}\tfrac12(X_j - iY_j)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\tfrac12(X - iY) = \begin{psmallmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix} = \ket1\bra0$ fills an empty orbital. The string $Z_0Z_1$ counts the parity of the orbitals \emph{before}
$j = 2$ and supplies the sign $(-1)^{n_0 + n_1}$ that makes operators on different orbitals \emph{anti}commute. Result: $\tfrac12 Z_0Z_1X_2 - \tfrac i2Z_0Z_1Y_2$
(OpenFermion gives the same: \texttt{ZZXI}: $0.5$, \texttt{ZZYI}: $-0.5i$). Without the string (option 2) $\{a_0, a_2^\dagger\}$ would not vanish;
$\tfrac12(X + iY)$ is the annihilation operator.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $\frac12(X + iY)$ annihilates.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Without the $Z$ string fermionic anticommutation fails.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] The string runs over \emph{earlier} qubits, not later ones.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} JW = local occupation + non-local parity string.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{62}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{JW hopping term}
Under Jordan--Wigner, the hopping term $a_0^\dagger a_1 + a_1^\dagger a_0$ between neighbouring spin-orbitals 0 and 1 becomes
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$X_0X_1$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$\tfrac12(X_0X_1 + Y_0Y_1)$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$\tfrac12(Z_0 + Z_1)$ & \optlabel{D}\,$\tfrac12(X_0X_1 - Y_0Y_1)$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $\tfrac12(X_0X_1 + Y_0Y_1)$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Hopping terms under Jordan--Wigner.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $a_j^\dagger a_{j+1} + \text{h.c.} = \tfrac12(X_jX_{j+1} + Y_jY_{j+1})$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $a_0^\dagger = \tfrac12(X_0 - iY_0)$ and $a_1 = Z_0\,\tfrac12(X_1 + iY_1)$ (the Jordan--Wigner string of orbital 1 is $Z_0$). Since
$(X - iY)Z = XZ - iYZ = -iY + X$, we get $(X_0 - iY_0)Z_0 = X_0 - iY_0$, so
\[ a_0^\dagger a_1 = \tfrac14(X_0 - iY_0)(X_1 + iY_1) = \tfrac14\big(X_0X_1 + Y_0Y_1 + iX_0Y_1 - iY_0X_1\big). \]
The Hermitian conjugate $a_1^\dagger a_0$ has the opposite imaginary parts, so the sum is $\tfrac12(X_0X_1 + Y_0Y_1)$. It swaps $\ket{01} \leftrightarrow \ket{10}$ (one electron
hops) and annihilates $\ket{00}$, $\ket{11}$. Verified with OpenFermion (\texttt{XX}: $0.5$, \texttt{YY}: $0.5$). $\tfrac12(X_0X_1 - Y_0Y_1)$ would create or destroy \emph{pairs}.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $X_0X_1$ alone also flips $\ket{00} \leftrightarrow \ket{11}$, changing electron number.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $Z$ terms are number operators, not hopping.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $XX - YY$ is the pairing term $a^\dagger a^\dagger + aa$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Neighbouring hops are short; distant hops carry $Z$ strings.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{63}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{JW vs.\ BK Pauli weight}
The Pauli weight (number of non-identity factors) of the image of $a_7^\dagger$ on 8 spin-orbitals is ... under Jordan--Wigner and ... under Bravyi--Kitaev.
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$8$; $4$ & \optlabel{B}\,$8$; $8$ & \optlabel{C}\,$1$; $4$ & \optlabel{D}\,$4$; $8$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $8$; $4$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Pauli weight of encodings.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} JW: weight $j + 1$ for $a_j^\dagger$; BK: $O(\log_2N)$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Jordan--Wigner stores occupations locally but the parity of all previous orbitals non-locally: $a_7^\dagger = Z_0\cdots Z_6\,\tfrac12(X_7 - iY_7)$, weight $7 + 1 = 8$ --- $O(N)$.
Bravyi--Kitaev stores partial sums of occupations in a binary-tree pattern so that both occupation and parity information are spread over only
$O(\log N)$ qubits; for $N = 8$ the strings of $a_7^\dagger$ have weight $\log_28 + 1 = 4$ (OpenFermion: maximum weight 4). Lower weight means
shorter circuits for $e^{i\theta P}$ on hardware. The notebook uses neither mapping explicitly; its H$_2$ coefficients are already Jordan--Wigner.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] BK reduces the weight.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Weight 1 ignores the parity string.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Reversed: Jordan--Wigner has the long string (weight 8), Bravyi--Kitaev the short one (weight 4).
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} BK trades simplicity for logarithmic locality.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{64}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Fermion encodings}
Match each fermion-to-qubit encoding (List-I) with its characteristic property (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & Jordan--Wigner & \textbf{(1)} & qubit $j$ stores the parity $n_0 \oplus\dots\oplus n_j$; total parity and $S_z$-parity sit on single qubits, so two qubits can be removed \\
\textbf{(Q)} & Bravyi--Kitaev & \textbf{(2)} & symmetries ($\mathbb Z_2$ stabilisers commuting with $H$) are used to remove qubits from any encoding \\
\textbf{(R)} & parity mapping & \textbf{(3)} & qubit $j$ stores the occupation $n_j$; strings of length $O(N)$ \\
\textbf{(S)} & qubit tapering & \textbf{(4)} & qubits store partial sums of occupations on a binary tree; strings of length $O(\log N)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$3, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 & \correctlabel{B}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$2 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$2, S$\to$1
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} P$\to$3, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$2

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Fermion encodings and symmetry reductions.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} JW: $q_j = n_j$; parity: $q_j = \bigoplus_{k\le j}n_k$; BK: tree partial sums.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item P: Jordan--Wigner: occupation basis, $Z$-strings (3).
\item Q: Bravyi--Kitaev: binary-tree partial sums, logarithmic weight (4).
\item R: parity mapping: cumulative parities; with interleaved/blocked spin ordering the electron-number parity and spin parity become single-qubit
$Z$'s, which allows the well-known reduction of H$_2$ from 4 to 2 qubits (1).
\item S: tapering (Bravyi et al.\ 2017) is a general symmetry reduction applied after any encoding (2).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] P$\to$4, Q$\to$3 swaps JW and BK.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Q$\to$1, R$\to$4 swaps BK and parity.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] R$\to$2, S$\to$1 swaps parity mapping and tapering.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Choice of encoding changes circuit cost, not physics.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{65}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Bravyi--Kitaev encoding}
For 4 modes, the Bravyi--Kitaev qubit values are $b = Bn \bmod 2$ with $B = \begin{psmallmatrix}1&0&0&0\\1&1&0&0\\0&0&1&0\\1&1&1&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ and $n$ the occupation vector.
The Hartree--Fock occupation $n = (1, 1, 0, 0)$ is encoded as
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$\ket{0100}$ & \optlabel{B}\,$\ket{1100}$ & \optlabel{C}\,$\ket{1101}$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$\ket{1000}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $\ket{1000}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Bravyi--Kitaev encoding of occupations.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $b = Bn \bmod 2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $b_0 = n_0 = 1$; $b_1 = n_0 + n_1 = 2 \equiv 0$; $b_2 = n_2 = 0$; $b_3 = n_0 + n_1 + n_2 + n_3 = 2 \equiv 0$. So $\ket{1000}$.
Check with OpenFermion: the Bravyi--Kitaev Hamiltonian of H$_2$ has $\braket{1000|H_{\mathrm{BK}}|1000} = E_{\mathrm{HF}}$, while $\braket{1100|H_{\mathrm{BK}}|1100}$ is a different
energy. The same physical state has different bitstrings in different encodings --- an ansatz must start from the encoding-correct reference.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $\ket{0100}$ has $b_0 = 0$, but the first BK qubit equals $n_0 = 1$.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] That is the JW bitstring.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $b_3 = 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 0 \pmod 2$, not 1.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Reference states must be re-encoded for each mapping.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{66}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{UCCSD excitation count}
Counting excitations in spin-orbitals without spin restrictions, LiH in STO-3G (12 spin-orbitals, 4 electrons) has how many single and double
excitations from the Hartree--Fock determinant?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$32$ singles and $168$ doubles & \optlabel{B}\,$32$ singles and $1024$ doubles \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$8$ singles and $28$ doubles & \optlabel{D}\,$48$ singles and $168$ doubles
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $32$ singles and $168$ doubles

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Counting UCCSD excitations.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} singles $n_on_v$; doubles $\binom{n_o}{2}\binom{n_v}{2}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Occupied spin-orbitals $n_{\mathrm{occ}} = 4$, virtual $n_{\mathrm{virt}} = 12 - 4 = 8$. Singles: choose one occupied and one virtual: $4\times8 = 32$.
Doubles: choose two occupied and two virtual: $\binom42\binom82 = 6\times28 = 168$. UCCSD has one parameter per excitation (fewer if spin and
spatial symmetry are imposed). For H$_2$: $\binom22\binom22 = 1$ double --- the notebook's single parameter.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1024 = 32^2$ squares the singles.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Spatial-orbital counts without spin.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $48 = 4\times12$ includes occupied targets.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} UCCSD parameters grow like $n_o^2n_v^2$.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{67}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{JW double excitation}
Under Jordan--Wigner, the anti-Hermitian double-excitation generator $a_3^\dagger a_2^\dagger a_1a_0 - a_0^\dagger a_1^\dagger a_2a_3$ becomes a sum of how many Pauli strings,
and what does the notebook's UCC kernel use?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] 4 strings with coefficients $\pm\tfrac12$; the notebook keeps $\texttt{XXYY}$
\item[\optlabel{B}] 1 string; the notebook uses all of it
\item[\correctlabel{C}] 8 strings with coefficients $\pm i/8$; the notebook keeps the single string $\texttt{XXXY}$
\item[\optlabel{D}] 16 strings; the notebook keeps 8
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} 8 strings with coefficients $\pm i/8$; the notebook keeps the single string $\texttt{XXXY}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} JW form of excitation operators.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $a^\dagger a^\dagger aa - \text{h.c.} = \frac i8\sum_{8\text{ strings}}\pm P$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Each of the four operators contributes $\tfrac12(X \mp iY)$, giving $2^4 = 16$ products; the Hermitian conjugate cancels half of them, leaving 8 strings
with an odd number of $Y$'s and coefficients $\pm i/8$ (OpenFermion: $\texttt{XXXY}, \texttt{XXYX}, \texttt{XYXX}, \texttt{YXXX}, \texttt{XYYY}, \dots$). Full UCC
would exponentiate all 8 (they commute, so $e^{\theta(T - T^\dagger)}$ factorises exactly). The notebook keeps only $e^{i\theta\,\texttt{XXXY}}$: starting from $\ket{1100}$ it
already rotates within $\mathrm{span}\{\ket{1100}, \ket{0011}\}$ (Q.31), which contains the exact ground state (Q.49), so nothing is lost for H$_2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Coefficients are $\pm i/8$ and the strings have an odd number of $Y$'s; $\texttt{XXYY}$ is a Hamiltonian term.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Four ladder operators give 16 products, 8 survive.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Half of the 16 cancel against the conjugate.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Problem-specific shortcuts are fine when they keep the exact subspace.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{68}
\qmeta{Matching lists}{Obstacles and remedies}
Match each practical VQE difficulty (List-I) with a standard remedy (List-II).
\par\smallskip\noindent{\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}%
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}c>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.33\linewidth}@{\hspace{1.2em}}cL@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{List-I}} & \multicolumn{2}{l@{}}{\textbf{List-II}} \\ \midrule
\textbf{(P)} & barren plateaus (vanishing gradients for deep random circuits) & \textbf{(1)} & error mitigation, e.g.\ zero-noise extrapolation \\
\textbf{(Q)} & shot noise in energy estimates & \textbf{(2)} & chemically motivated ansatz, local cost functions, careful (e.g.\ Hartree--Fock) initialisation \\
\textbf{(R)} & gate errors on hardware & \textbf{(3)} & several restarts / good initial parameters \\
\textbf{(S)} & local minima of $E(\boldsymbol\theta)$ & \textbf{(4)} & measurement grouping and more shots for terms with large $|c_k|$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}}
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,P$\to$4, Q$\to$2, R$\to$1, S$\to$3 & \correctlabel{B}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3 \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$1, R$\to$4, S$\to$3 & \optlabel{D}\,P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$3, S$\to$1
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} P$\to$2, Q$\to$4, R$\to$1, S$\to$3

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Practical VQE obstacles.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\mathrm{Var}[\partial_\theta E] \sim 2^{-n}$ (barren plateau); SE $\propto 1/\sqrt S$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item P: barren plateaus (McClean et al.\ 2018): gradient variance decays exponentially with $n$ for random deep ansätze; structured ansätze, local cost
functions and good initialisation help (2).
\item Q: shot noise $\propto \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}/S}$: group commuting terms, allocate shots by $|c_k|$ (4).
\item R: gate noise biases the energy upwards; mitigation such as zero-noise extrapolation (Q.72) (1).
\item S: local minima: multiple starts, Hartree--Fock or INTERP-like initialisation (3).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] P$\to$4, Q$\to$2 swaps barren plateaus and shot noise.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Q$\to$1, R$\to$4 swaps shot noise and gate errors.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] R$\to$3, S$\to$1 swaps gate errors and local minima.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Each obstacle has its own remedy; none is free.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{69}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Shots for chemical accuracy}
An energy estimator has a per-shot standard deviation of $0.1$ Ha. How many shots are needed for a standard error of $1.6$ mHa (chemical accuracy)?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,about $1.6\times10^{5}$ & \optlabel{B}\,about $63$ & \correctlabel{C}\,about $3.9\times10^3$ & \optlabel{D}\,about $2.6\times10^{-4}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} about $3.9\times10^3$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Shot count for a target precision.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $S = (\sigma/\varepsilon)^2$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $\mathrm{SE} = \sigma/\sqrt S \le 0.0016 \Rightarrow S \ge (0.1/0.0016)^2 = 62.5^2 = 3906$. $63$ forgets to square. Precision costs quadratically: halving
the error needs four times the shots, and every optimizer step needs such an estimate --- the main practical cost of VQE on hardware.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $1.6\times10^5$ uses $\varepsilon = 0.25$ mHa.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $63 = \sigma/\varepsilon$, not squared.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $2.6\times10^{-4} = (\varepsilon/\sigma)^2$ inverts the ratio; a shot count must be large when $\varepsilon \ll \sigma$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Ten times more precision costs a hundred times more shots.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{70}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Fully depolarised energy}
Under complete depolarisation the state becomes $\rho = I/2^n$. For the notebook's 4-qubit H$_2$ Hamiltonian the measured energy would then be
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$-0.0971$ Ha, the coefficient of $\texttt{IIII}$ & \optlabel{B}\,$-1.1168$ Ha \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$-1.1373$ Ha & \optlabel{D}\,$0$ Ha
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $-0.0971$ Ha, the coefficient of $\texttt{IIII}$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Maximally mixed state energy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\operatorname{tr}(H)/2^n = c_{I\dots I}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $E = \operatorname{tr}(\rho H) = 2^{-n}\operatorname{tr}H = \sum_kc_k\,2^{-n}\operatorname{tr}P_k = c_{IIII}$, since every non-identity Pauli string is traceless. Here $-0.0970663$ Ha.
Noise thus pulls the energy \emph{up} towards $c_{IIII}$, far above $E_{\mathrm{FCI}} = -1.1373$; partial depolarisation interpolates between the ideal
value and this limit.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] HF needs the pure state $\ket{1100}$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] FCI needs the ideal ground state.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] The identity coefficient is not zero.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Noise drags energies towards the identity coefficient.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{71}
\qmeta{Assertion--Reason}{Variational bound vs.\ shot noise}
\textbf{Assertion (A):} With a finite number of shots, an estimated VQE energy can never fall below $E_0$.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Reason (R):} For every density matrix $\rho$ (pure or mixed, noisy or not), $\operatorname{tr}(\rho H) \ge E_0$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both A and R are true, but R is \emph{not} the correct explanation of A
\item[\optlabel{C}] A is true, but R is false
\item[\correctlabel{D}] A is false, but R is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} A is false, but R is true

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Variational principle for mixed states versus sampling noise.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $\operatorname{tr}(\rho H) \ge E_0$; estimator SE $\sigma/\sqrt S$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{R is true:} $\rho = \sum_jp_j\ket{\psi_j}\bra{\psi_j}$ with $p_j \ge 0$, $\sum p_j = 1$, so $\operatorname{tr}(\rho H) = \sum_jp_j\braket{\psi_j|H|\psi_j} \ge E_0$: the variational principle survives noise.
\textbf{A is false:} a finite-shot \emph{estimate} fluctuates around $\operatorname{tr}(\rho H)$ with standard error $\sigma/\sqrt S$, and can fall below $E_0$ when the true value is
close to it. The notebook warns about this (``only shot noise can push single evaluations slightly below''). Answer: (D).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] needs A true, R true \emph{and} R explaining A; A is false.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] needs A and R both true but R not explaining A; A is false.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] needs A true and R false; A is false and R true.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} The true expectation obeys the bound; finite-shot estimates may not.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{72}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Zero-noise extrapolation}
Zero-noise extrapolation: an energy measured at noise scale factors $\lambda = 1$ and $\lambda = 3$ gives $-1.10$ Ha and $-1.00$ Ha. A linear extrapolation to
$\lambda = 0$ gives
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$-1.10$ Ha & \correctlabel{B}\,$-1.15$ Ha & \optlabel{C}\,$-1.05$ Ha & \optlabel{D}\,$-1.20$ Ha
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $-1.15$ Ha

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Zero-noise extrapolation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $E(0) = E(\lambda_1) - \lambda_1\frac{E(\lambda_2) - E(\lambda_1)}{\lambda_2 - \lambda_1}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Slope: $\frac{-1.00 - (-1.10)}{3 - 1} = 0.05$ Ha per unit $\lambda$. $E(0) = E(1) - 0.05 = -1.15$ Ha. Extrapolation removes the bias of noise but amplifies
statistical errors, and the extrapolated value carries \emph{no} variational guarantee: it can land below $E_0$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Value at $\lambda = 1$, not extrapolated.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Wrong direction: noise raises the energy.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Extrapolates by the full difference twice.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Mitigated energies lose the variational guarantee.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{73}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{GPU request without GPU}
\texttt{VQE.ipynb} is run with \texttt{BACKEND = "gpu"} on a machine where \texttt{cudaq.num\_available\_gpus()} returns 0. What happens?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] The notebook runs on the GPU emulator \texttt{tensornet} instead
\item[\optlabel{B}] CUDA-Q silently falls back to \texttt{qpp-cpu}
\item[\correctlabel{C}] \texttt{resolve\_backend} raises a \texttt{RuntimeError} explaining that no NVIDIA GPU is visible; no GPU target is selected
\item[\optlabel{D}] The run starts and crashes later with an out-of-memory error
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} \texttt{resolve\_backend} raises a \texttt{RuntimeError} explaining that no NVIDIA GPU is visible; no GPU target is selected

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Backend safety checks in the shared utilities.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} \texttt{if backend in ("gpu", "multi-gpu") and num\_gpus == 0: raise RuntimeError}.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The shared utilities check \texttt{if backend in ("gpu", "multi-gpu") and num\_gpus == 0} and raise \texttt{RuntimeError("BACKEND='gpu' was requested but CUDA-Q
sees no NVIDIA GPU ...")}. GPU targets are never selected without a GPU because selecting \texttt{tensornet} on such a machine aborted the
Python process (README, known limitations). Only \texttt{BACKEND = "auto"} falls back to the CPU. GPU paths are implemented but were not executed.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] No GPU target is ever selected without a GPU.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Only \texttt{"auto"} falls back to CPU.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] The check happens before any simulation.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Explicit backend requests fail loudly, as they should.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{74}
\qmeta{Statement I / II}{Exact references}
\textbf{Statement I:} For the Ising chain, the notebook computes its reference energy by sparse diagonalisation for every $N$.\\[1mm]
\textbf{Statement II:} For \texttt{"H2"} and \texttt{"custom"} Hamiltonians, an exact reference is computed only up to \texttt{REFERENCE\_MAX\_QUBITS = 18} qubits.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] Both Statement I and Statement II are true
\item[\optlabel{B}] Both Statement I and Statement II are false
\item[\optlabel{C}] Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
\item[\correctlabel{D}] Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} Statement I is false, but Statement II is true

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Exact references in the notebook.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} TFIM: free fermions (any $N$); others: \texttt{eigsh} for $N \le 18$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} \textbf{I is false:} the Ising reference uses the free-fermion formula \texttt{tfim\_exact\_energy} for any $N$; sparse diagonalisation is only an
\emph{additional cross-check} for $N \le 16$ (it printed $-15.0825179883$, identical).
\textbf{II is true:} \texttt{elif n\_qubits <= REFERENCE\_MAX\_QUBITS: reference\_energy = exact\_ground\_energy\_sparse(...)}; above that, ``not computed''. Answer: (D).

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] needs both statements true; I is false.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] needs both statements false; II is true.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] needs I true and II false; I is false and II true.
\end{itemize}

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{75}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Free-fermion matrix size}
The notebook's exact Ising reference maps the chain to free fermions and computes $E_0 = -\tfrac12\sum|\lambda(iA)|$ for a real antisymmetric matrix $A$. For
$N = 100$ qubits, $A$ has size
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$4\times4$ & \correctlabel{B}\,$200\times200$ & \optlabel{C}\,$100\times100$ & \optlabel{D}\,$2^{100}\times2^{100}$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{B}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(B)}} $200\times200$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Free-fermion solution of the Ising chain.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $2N$ Majorana modes; $E_0 = -\frac12\sum|\lambda(iA)|$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Each spin becomes two Majorana operators ($a_j$, $b_j$), so $A$ is $2N\times2N$: $200\times200$, diagonalised in milliseconds. The Hamiltonian matrix
would be $2^{100}\times2^{100}$ --- impossible to store. Exactly solvable models give VQE benchmarks at any size; molecules generally do not.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Constant size only for $N = 2$.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Forgets the two Majoranas per site.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] That is the Hilbert-space dimension.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Integrable models give exact large-$N$ benchmarks.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{76}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Recorded timing}
In the recorded run the quantum execution time was $69.10$ s for $300$ energy evaluations, while the notebook's pre-run estimate was $\sim102.9$ s.
The average time per evaluation, and the ratio estimate/measured cell time ($70.1$ s), are about
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$0.0032$ s and $1.5$ & \optlabel{B}\,$69$ s and $1.5$ \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$0.23$ s and $0.68$ & \correctlabel{D}\,$0.23$ s and $1.5$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{D}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(D)}} $0.23$ s and $1.5$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Timing analysis of a recorded run.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $t_{\mathrm{eval}} = t_{\mathrm{exec}}/N_{\mathrm{eval}}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} $69.10/300 = 0.230$ s per \texttt{cudaq.observe} call (73-gate circuit, 29 terms, 15 qubits). $102.9/70.1 = 1.47$: the estimate was about $50\,\%$ high,
within the stated $\pm3\times$ (it assumed an extra state pass for the energy, ``x2 rough allowance''). $0.0032$ s is the time per \emph{gate}
($0.230/73$), not per evaluation; $0.68$ is the inverse ratio.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $0.0032$ s is per gate.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $69$ s is the total execution time of all 300 evaluations, not the time of one.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.68$ is measured/estimate.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Estimates are rough; measured timings are the benchmark.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{77}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{Frozen core}
For LiH (STO-3G, 12 spin-orbitals under Jordan--Wigner), freezing the doubly occupied Li $1s$ core orbital removes how many qubits?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{2}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$2$, leaving $10$ qubits & \optlabel{B}\,$0$; frozen orbitals still need qubits \\[3pt]
\optlabel{C}\,$4$, leaving $8$ qubits & \optlabel{D}\,$1$, leaving $11$ qubits
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $2$, leaving $10$ qubits

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Frozen core approximation.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} qubits removed $= 2\times$ frozen spatial orbitals.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} One spatial orbital = two spin-orbitals ($\alpha$, $\beta$) = two qubits under Jordan--Wigner. Freezing it (always occupied, absorbed into the constant and
one-body terms) leaves $12 - 2 = 10$ qubits and 2 active electrons. Further symmetry tapering and removing weakly occupied virtual orbitals reduce the
count further; every such reduction is an approximation choice except tapering, which is exact.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Frozen orbitals are removed from the active space.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] Only one orbital is frozen.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Spin doubles the count.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Active spaces trade accuracy for qubits.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{78}
\qmeta{Single-correct MCQ}{LiH Pauli terms}
Generated with PySCF and OpenFermion (STO-3G, Jordan--Wigner, bond length 1.595 \AA), the LiH qubit Hamiltonian has how many Pauli terms, compared with
15 for H$_2$?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\optlabel{A}\,$4096$ & \optlabel{B}\,$144$ & \correctlabel{C}\,$631$ & \optlabel{D}\,$30$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} $631$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Growth of molecular Pauli sums.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} $O(N^4)$ terms; LiH/STO-3G/JW: 631.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} The number of terms grows like $N^4$ (Q.12): from $N = 4$ to $N = 12$ spin-orbitals the naive factor is $3^4 = 81$; symmetries remove many, and the
generated Hamiltonian has 631 Pauli terms (checked in \texttt{verify\_answers.py}). $4096 = 2^{12}$ is the dimension of the state, not a term count.
More terms mean more measurement settings and shots per energy evaluation, the dominant cost of molecular VQE.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] $2^{12}$ is the state dimension.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $144 = 12^2$ counts only one-body terms.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Far too few for 12 qubits with all two-electron integrals.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Measurement cost, not qubit count, dominates molecular VQE.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{20\baselineskip}
\begin{passagebox}{Paragraph for Questions 79 and 80}
\emph{Previously recorded default run of \texttt{VQE.ipynb}} (CUDA-Q 0.16.0, target \texttt{qpp-cpu}, 4 vCPU): Ising chain with $N = 15$, $J = 1$,
$h = 0.5$ (29 Pauli terms); hardware-efficient ansatz with 2 layers (45 parameters, 73 gates); COBYLA stopped with ``the objective function has
been evaluated MAXFUN times'' after 300 evaluations; $E_{\mathrm{VQE}} = -15.0533898284$, exact $E_0 = -15.0825179883$; quantum execution time
$69.10$ s; the optimised state gave $\ket{000\dots0}$ with probability $0.7005$. The product state $\ket{000\dots0}$ itself has energy $-14$.
\end{passagebox}
\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{79}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Recorded run: recovered fraction}
Measured from the product state $\ket{000\dots0}$ ($E = -14$), what fraction of the remaining energy gap to $E_0$ did VQE recover?
\par\smallskip\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}*{4}{L}@{}}
\correctlabel{A}\,$97.3\,\%$ & \optlabel{B}\,$99.8\,\%$ & \optlabel{C}\,$70.1\,\%$ & \optlabel{D}\,$2.7\,\%$
\end{tabularx}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{A}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(A)}} $97.3\,\%$

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Baseline-normalised accuracy.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} fraction $= \frac{E_{\mathrm{base}} - E_{\mathrm{VQE}}}{E_{\mathrm{base}} - E_0}$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} Gap from the product state to $E_0$: $-14 - (-15.0825180) = 1.0825180$. Recovered: $-14 - (-15.0533898) = 1.0533898$.
Fraction $1.0533898/1.0825180 = 0.973$. The relative error $0.193\,\%$ (Q.55) looks tiny because most of the energy ($-14$) comes from the trivial
ordered state; measured against this baseline the ansatz still misses $2.7\,\%$ of the quantum-fluctuation energy. $99.8\,\%$ is $1 - 0.193\,\%$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(B)}] $1 - 0.193\,\%$ ignores the baseline.
\item[\textbf{(C)}] $0.70$ is the probability of $\ket{0\dots0}$.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] $2.7\,\%$ is the missing fraction.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Measure progress against a trivial reference.
\end{solbox}
\qsep

\needspace{13\baselineskip}
\begin{qitem}{80}
\qmeta{Paragraph based}{Recorded run: next step}
Which change is most likely to reduce the remaining error of this run?
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em, labelsep=0.4em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item[\optlabel{A}] More final sampling shots
\item[\optlabel{B}] Switching from the free-fermion reference to sparse diagonalisation
\item[\correctlabel{C}] More evaluations (the budget was exhausted) and, if needed, more ansatz layers
\item[\optlabel{D}] Reducing \texttt{MAX\_EVALUATIONS} to stop earlier
\end{itemize}
\end{qitem}
\begin{solbox}{C}
\textbf{\color{brand}Correct answer.} \textcolor{okgreen}{\textbf{(C)}} More evaluations (the budget was exhausted) and, if needed, more ansatz layers

\textbf{\color{brand}Concepts required.} Diagnosing a VQE run.

\textbf{\color{brand}Relevant formulae.} budget exhausted $\Rightarrow$ not converged; expressiveness grows with $L$.

\textbf{\color{brand}Step-by-step explanation.} COBYLA stopped because of \texttt{MAXFUN}, not because of a convergence criterion, so the optimiser had not finished; a 2-layer ansatz may also lack
expressiveness (the notebook suggests more layers and evaluations, e.g.\ 4 layers and 800 evaluations for the harder critical point). The final
sampling only displays bitstrings; it does not change the energy. Both references are exact and agree to $10^{-10}$. Fewer evaluations can only
make the error larger or equal.

\textbf{\color{brand}Why the other options are incorrect.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.4em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item[\textbf{(A)}] Sampling shots do not change the optimised energy.
\item[\textbf{(B)}] Both references are exact and agree.
\item[\textbf{(D)}] Fewer evaluations cannot help.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{\color{brand}Key takeaway.} Read the optimizer's stopping message before trusting the energy.
\end{solbox}
